findings.title: creditInternal is the only one of the three primitives with no atomicity — wallet, Transaction and ledger are three independent autocommits outside the lock's transaction
findings.whatTheCodeDoes: `debitInternal` (wallet-service.ts:1996-2018) and `adminAdjustBalance` (wallet-service.ts:2075-2093) both wrap their wallet mutation, their Transaction row and their `postLedgerEntries` call in `withMoneyTx(async (tx) => …)` and pass `tx` down to all three. `creditInternal` wraps nothing: `db.wallet.adjust(wallet.id, { balance: amount })` (1888), `db.txn.create({…})` (1890-1915) and `postLedgerEntries(\`int_${txnId}\`, lines).catch(() => {})` (1924) are each issued with no `tx` argument, so each takes `pc()` — the global Prisma client — and autocommits on its own connection.
findings.whyItIsWrong: `withLock` in production opens a real `$transaction` and publishes it for exactly this purpose (locks.ts:127-138), and its own contract says (locks.ts:161-163) "Everything inside ONE withLock now shares ONE transaction, so a throw rolls back every write made under the lock." That statement is false for creditInternal, which never uses the tx the lock hands it. debitInternal's doc-block asserts the discipline the file believes is universal — "Money-safe: wallet + txn + ledger commit ATOMICALLY (withMoneyTx) inside the wallet lock, exactly as `adminAdjustBalance` does" (wallet-service.ts:1948-1949) — and creditInternal is the exception nobody wrote down. This is the structural cause of MO-10.a and it has a second, independent failure direction: the wallet can move while the Transaction row does not.
findings.rulesReference: none - internal consistency (the file's own money-safety contract at wallet-service.ts:1948-1949 and 2043-2046, and locks.ts:161-163)
findings.concreteScenario: Same agent A / TZS 100,000 stake / net accrual TZS 605. This time the wallet UPDATE succeeds (A's balance 0 → 605) and `db.txn.create` throws on the next statement (transient DB fault). The throw escapes creditInternal, escapes `creditWallet`, escapes `onRecruitSettlement`, and is swallowed by market-service.ts:3817-3820 `catch (err) { accrualsErrored++; audit(... "affiliate.settlement_accrual_error" ...) }`. Result: A's wallet holds TZS 605 with no Transaction row, no ledger group (line 1924 is never reached), and no ReferralReward row. The accrual is invisible to the per-recruit cap, to A's own statement, and to `clawbackMarketCommission` — if that market is later voided, the 605 cannot be reversed because `listByMarket` finds no row. And it will never be re-attempted: a resumed settlement re-reads only still-OPEN positions (market-service.ts:3694-3695: "A resumed settlement's loop sees only the still-OPEN positions"), and this position is already settled.
findings.moneyImpact: TZS 605 leaves the house permanently unrecorded and unclawbackable, per occurrence. In the opposite direction (MO-10.a) the same missing transaction boundary loses the agent the money. Either way the wallet, the Transaction table and the ledger can disagree by the full credit amount, and the wallet↔ledger reconciliation (`trialBalance`, ledger.ts:806-841) reports the drift with no cause. Applies to every internal credit: agent commission, player-promo referral bonuses/prizes, and proposal prizes.

findings.title: The two-person rule on large balance adjustments can be executed more than once from a single first approval — the stage-1 clearance is not propagated and the check has no lock
findings.whatTheCodeDoes: Stage-1 approvals for adjustments ≥ TZS 1,000,000 are held in a per-process `Map` mirrored to a SystemConfig row. `getAdjustStage1` returns the in-process entry without ever re-reading the database when one is present, and has no expiry. `setAdjustStage1(userId, null)` — the clearance after a countersigned execution — deletes only the executing process's Map entry. There is no lock anywhere around read-stage-1 → check → `adminAdjustBalance` → clear.
findings.whyItIsWrong: Two separate holes, both visible against this repo's own siblings. (1) Cross-instance: `withLock`/locks.ts is built on the premise of multiple Railway instances ("Safe across multiple Railway instances") and purge-stage1-store.ts:69-72 is explicit that a stale mirror must be dropped — it carries a TTL and does `else mem.delete(chainId)` on a stale persisted read. `getAdjustStage1` has neither, so a replica that cached the first approval keeps serving it forever after another replica executed and cleared it. (2) TOCTOU: the AML twin wraps exactly this sequence in a lock and says why, at aml/actions.ts:69-70 — "Lock the transaction to prevent TOCTOU — two officers clicking approve at once could otherwise both pass the AML_REVIEW check and bypass the two-person rule." The balance-adjust path has no lock, and unlike the AML path there is no state transition (a txn leaving AML_REVIEW) to make a repeat inert. Additionally `setAdjustStage1(userId, null)` passes plain `null` into `saveConfig`, whose target column is `value Json` (non-nullable, schema.prisma:2307-2311); this repo already documents that a bare null into a Json column is wrong (ai-poll-generation.ts:35-37, guarded by retention.test.mts:276) and `saveConfig` swallows any failure (config-store.ts:65-67), so whether the durable half is ever cleared cannot be settled from the repo.
findings.rulesReference: none - internal consistency (the two-person control asserted in the wrapper's own comment at actions.ts:271-281 and in wallet-service.ts:2046-2049; parity with the AML two-person rule at aml/constants.ts:1-10)
findings.concreteScenario: Officer A proposes a credit of TZS 1,000,000 to player P; the request lands on replica 1, which records the stage-1 record in its own Map and in SystemConfig. Officer B submits the identical credit; it lands on replica 2, which loads the record from SystemConfig, sees `first.actorId !== B` and `first.signed === signed`, executes `adminAdjustBalance(P, B, +1_000_000, reason)` — P's balance rises by 1,000,000 — then clears replica 2's Map and the DB row. Replica 1's Map still holds Officer A's stage-1 record and will never re-read the database. Any later submission of the same +1,000,000 for P that routes to replica 1, by B or by any officer other than A, passes both checks against that stale record and executes immediately: a second TZS 1,000,000 credit with no fresh first approval and no second signature. The same outcome arrives on a single instance if two countersign submissions overlap, since nothing serialises the read-check-execute.
findings.moneyImpact: TZS 1,000,000 (and up to the TZS 50,000,000 single-adjustment cap) can leave the house on one officer's action where the control promises two, and repeatedly. A debit of the same shape takes the money off a player with one signature. Because each execution audits as `balance_adjust.countersigned` naming a first officer who did not approve this movement, the audit trail reads as a clean two-person ceremony.

findings.title: The 30-minute "never terminalise a payout early" grace is measured from `createdAt`, so an AML-approved payout is inside the reversal-capable sweep from the instant it is dispatched — and is permanently excluded from the confirm-only fast lane by the same field
findings.whatTheCodeDoes: Both payout lanes select on `createdAt`. `isFastPayoutCandidate` returns true only for `at >= nowMs - fastWindowMs` (30 min), and `reconcileStalePayments` selects `Date.parse(t.createdAt) < cutoff` (now − 30 min). Neither looks at when the payout was actually dispatched, and no `dispatchedAt` column is read anywhere on this path.
findings.whyItIsWrong: For an ordinary payout the two windows tile correctly: for the first 30 minutes only the confirm-only lane (which the file states "can NEVER fail or reverse one… the worst case is that it does nothing") may touch it, and the reversal-capable sweep is deliberately patient. An AML-held withdrawal is created hours before it is dispatched — the two-officer rule at admin/aml/actions.ts requires two separate officers' clicks, so it is never dispatched within 30 minutes of creation. That inverts BOTH windows for every large payout: it is excluded from the confirm-only lane forever, and it enters the ONE path that can auto-reverse a payout with zero seconds of grace. The safety argument the 30-minute cutoff is built on ("a payout that is genuinely in flight at the gateway, blind-reversed here, would refund the player AND still pay out → double-pay", 1019-note) does not hold for exactly the class of payout where the money at stake is largest — ≥ TZS 1,000,000 by definition.
findings.rulesReference: none - internal consistency (the invariant is stated in this file's own headers for settleConfirmedWithdrawals and reconcileStalePayments)
findings.concreteScenario: A TZS 1,000,000 payout (fee 15,000, net 985,000) is created 09:00, approved and dispatched 11:20. Selcom accepts and returns `resultcode=111 INPROGRESS`. At 11:23 the sweep fires — three minutes after dispatch, where an ordinary payout would still have 27 minutes of protection — and asks /walletcashin/query about a transid Selcom accepted 180 seconds ago. If that record is not yet queryable and comes back with anything outside {000,111,927,999}, `envelopeSettlementVerdict` returns FAILED and line 1305 refunds 1,000,000 to the wallet while the 985,000 is on its way to the handset. Independently, the confirm side is degraded: even when everything works, the payout cannot be released by `settleConfirmedWithdrawals` at all (isFastPayoutCandidate is false for it), so the hold sits until a sweep tick.
findings.moneyImpact: TZS 985,000 paid twice per occurrence, on the highest-value payouts on the platform, with no crash and no stale ref required — only Selcom answering a just-accepted transid with a code outside the accepted set. Unlike MO-2.a this is not a narrow window: EVERY AML-approved payout spends its whole life in the reversal-capable lane with no grace period at all.

findings.title: `settleWithdrawalFailed` refunds and marks FAILED as two unguarded, non-atomic pool writes whose errors are swallowed to null — then reports success and emails "Withdrawal returned" either way
findings.whatTheCodeDoes: Inside the wallet lock it does `if (w) await db.wallet.adjust(w.id, { balance: amt, hold: -amt });` — return value discarded — then `await db.txn.update(txnId, { status: "FAILED", … })`, then returns the transaction. Neither call is passed a transaction client, so both take `pc()` (prisma-dal.ts:1281, 1366) — separate autocommitted pool writes, NOT enrolled in the lock's transaction (the lock's tx is only reachable via `currentLockTx()`, which the DAL never calls). In no-tx mode both DAL methods end with `try { return await run(); } catch { return null; }` — a DB error is swallowed and reported as a benign null. Truthiness of `done` (the transaction object, always truthy when the status check passed) then drives the audit row, the SSE balance push, the notification and the "Withdrawal returned" email.
findings.whyItIsWrong: The sibling function one screen up does it correctly and says why: `settleWithdrawalConfirmed` wraps the hold release, the status write and the ledger group in `withMoneyTx` and checks the adjust — "const upd = await db.wallet.adjust(…); if (!upd) throw new Error(`withdraw ${txnId}: wallet ${w.id} row missing`)" — with the comment "a ledger failure rolls the whole thing back … rather than dropping the hold with no ledger record". The reversal path, which is the ONE path that gives a player their money back, has neither the transaction nor the check. Both halves can fail independently and in opposite directions, and the function's own doc comment ("Exactly-once under the wallet lock", "the idempotency here is what makes a race with the sweep or a late callback safe") is only true while both writes succeed — the status write IS the idempotency, and its failure is silent.
findings.rulesReference: §2.8 — the player is charged the pool fee and the withdrawal fee and nothing else. A refund that is announced but not made is an uncharted deduction of the whole gross; a refund made twice is an uncharted credit.
findings.concreteScenario: Direction 1 (money stranded): player withdraws TZS 200,000 (fee 3,000, net 197,000; balance 200,000 → 0, hold 200,000). All rails refuse definitively → withdraw() line 1754 calls settleWithdrawalFailed. Under load the wallet `updateMany` hits a P2024 pool timeout; `adjust` swallows it and returns null, which nobody reads. `db.txn.update` succeeds → status FAILED (terminal — no sweep ever revisits a FAILED row) and the player receives "Withdrawal returned · TZS 197,000". Their 200,000 is still sitting in `hold`: not spendable, not withdrawable, and `retryWithdrawalAction` on that FAILED row calls `withdraw()` again, which is refused by the balance check because the balance is 0. TZS 200,000 lost to the player until a human hand-patches the wallet row. Direction 2 (paid twice): the adjust succeeds, the status write throws and is swallowed to null — the player has their 200,000 back but the txn is still PROCESSING, so the next sweep re-queries, gets FAILED again, and line 1305 credits another 200,000.
findings.moneyImpact: TZS 200,000 per occurrence, in whichever direction the failing write falls: either the player is told their money came back when it did not (and it is unrecoverable through any automatic path, because FAILED is terminal), or the house refunds the same withdrawal on every subsequent sweep tick until the status write finally lands. This repo already documents P2024/P2028 surfacing raw under pool pressure (locks.ts:36-40), and both writes here need a pool connection while the lock's own $transaction is pinning one.

findings.title: The payout path never pre-persists its gateway reference — the exact hardening the DEPOSIT path carries, on the direction where the money is actually leaving
findings.whatTheCodeDoes: `dispatchDeposit` accepts a caller-minted `correlationId` and `deposit()` persists it BEFORE the network call (wallet-service.ts:333-338), with the reason spelled out at 328-332: "a crash, a redeploy or a DB blip in that window left a genuinely paid deposit with no reference at all… Persisting first means the reference always exists from the moment the gateway could possibly have been told about it." `dispatchWithdrawal` takes no such parameter — it mints `const correlationId = `wdr_${randomId(10)}`` internally at line 178 and the caller learns it only from the returned result, which is written to the row after the gateway has answered (wallet-service.ts:1736 then 1777; and 742 then 770 on the approve path).
findings.whyItIsWrong: The transid is in the request body Selcom signs, so it is known before the request leaves — there is no technical reason it cannot be persisted first, and the money-IN path proves it. If the process dies, is redeployed, or loses its pool connection between Selcom accepting the payout and line 1777, the row is PROCESSING with `providerRef: null` for a payout that has already been made. Every recovery route is then blind: `reconcileStalePayments` correctly refuses to act (`if (!ref) { leftPending++; auditNeedsReviewOnce(…) }`, 1290) so it sits forever; Selcom's callback carries the real transid, `db.txn.findByProviderRef(ref)` finds nothing and the webhook route silently acks it — `if (!txn) return NextResponse.json({ ok: true, ignored: true, reason: "unknown-reference" })` (route.ts:244) with no needs-review row; and the only action that can clear it, `reverseStuckPayoutAction`, records `providerSays = "not asked (no provider reference)"` (payment-actions.ts:251) and proceeds to refund — its own header calls the re-query "the machine check, not just the officer's word… the last thing standing between an officer and a double payment", and here that check is structurally absent.
findings.rulesReference: none - internal consistency (the deposit path's stated invariant, applied asymmetrically)
findings.concreteScenario: Player withdraws TZS 500,000 (fee 7,500, net 492,500; hold 500,000). The ladder POSTs /walletcashin/process, Selcom returns 200 · resultcode=111 and queues the disbursement. Railway redeploys the container 200 ms later (or the `db.txn.update` at 1777 hits a pool timeout, which the DAL swallows to null — line 1777 does not check its return value either). The row is PROCESSING, providerRef NULL, payoutRail NULL. The 492,500 lands on the player's phone. The callback arrives with the real transid and is answered "ok, ignored, unknown-reference". Every 5-minute sweep writes one needs-review line and moves on. Days later an officer clears the queue with "Return to player", the machine check reports "not asked (no provider reference)", and settleWithdrawalFailed credits 500,000 back to the wallet.
findings.moneyImpact: TZS 500,000 paid twice (492,500 disbursed plus 500,000 re-credited), and the platform has no evidence anywhere that it ever dispatched the payout — no providerRef, no rail, and `withdraw.rail_attempt` audit rows written only after the same await (1782). Frequency is one crash/redeploy/pool-timeout landing inside a ~1–45 s window per payout; Railway deploys and P2024s are both routine in this repo's history.

findings.title: The refund credit's failure is swallowed and never checked — the player is emailed "Withdrawal returned" while the money stays locked in `hold` forever
findings.whatTheCodeDoes: Line 806 is `if (w) await db.wallet.adjust(w.id, { balance: amt, hold: -amt });` — the return value is discarded. Because no `tx` is passed, prisma-dal takes the self-committing branch at line 1300: `try { return await run(); } catch { return null; }`. A DB error on the credit therefore becomes a silent `null`. Execution falls straight through to line 807, which marks the transaction FAILED (terminal), and then to lines 810-824, which audit `withdraw.failed`, push `notifyWithdraw(... status: "FAILED" ...)` and send the player an email subjected `Withdrawal returned · ${formatTzs(refunded)}`. The wallet row `w` was read one line earlier, so `res.count === 0` cannot be the cause — a null here means the write threw.
findings.whyItIsWrong: Its twin does check. settleWithdrawalConfirmed line 618 is `if (!upd) throw new Error(...)` on the very same helper, precisely so a failed hold release aborts the movement. The FAILED path has neither the transaction, nor a guard (`requireHoldGte` is unused anywhere), nor the return check — three separate defences its sibling has and it does not. The result is a terminal transaction whose money never moved: status FAILED means `reconcileStalePayments` (PROCESSING only, line 1228) will never touch it, `reverseStuckPayoutAction` refuses it (`if (t.status !== "PROCESSING") return { ok: false, error: ... }`, payment-actions.ts:248), and `settleWithdrawalConfirmed` refuses it (line 600). Nothing in the system can ever return that money, and the player has been told in writing that it was returned. Under §2.8 the only things a player may be charged are the pool fee and the withdrawal fee; losing the entire withdrawal amount is a deduction that does not exist in the rules.
findings.rulesReference: §2.8 — "The pool fee … Withdrawal fee 1.5% of the amount withdrawn. Nothing else." A silently un-refunded reversal charges the player 100% of the withdrawal.
findings.concreteScenario: Player has TZS 400,000 spendable and withdraws TZS 150,000 (fee TZS 2,250, net TZS 147,750). withdraw() line 1630 commits balance 250,000 / hold 150,000. The payout fails at the gateway. settleWithdrawalFailed runs; line 806's `updateMany` hits a pool-exhaustion (P2024) or connection-reset error under load; prisma-dal.ts:1300 catches it and returns null; nothing checks. Line 807 succeeds: status FAILED. The player receives an in-app FAILED notice for TZS 150,000 and an email "Withdrawal returned · TZS 150,000". Their actual wallet is still balance 250,000 / hold 150,000. They are TZS 150,000 short of spendable money, permanently, with a terminal transaction row that no sweep and no operator tool will reopen. computeTrialBalance again sees nothing: walletReal = 250,000 + 150,000 = 400,000 = ledgerReal, realDrift 0, ok true.
findings.moneyImpact: The player permanently loses the full gross of their own withdrawal — TZS 150,000 in the scenario, up to TZS 1,000,000 at the AML threshold. Repeatable on every transient DB error during a reversal. Invisible to the nightly trial balance, so the first signal is a support ticket from a player who was told their money came back.

findings.title: rejectAmlAction has the same split commit — an officer's retry after a partial reject refunds a ≥TZS 1,000,000 payout twice, and its comment claims the opposite
findings.whatTheCodeDoes: The AML rejection credits the held funds back at line 167 and flips the transaction to FAILED at line 171. Neither call receives a transaction client, so — exactly as in MO-3.a — both run on the pooled client and auto-commit independently, even though the whole body sits inside `withLock('aml-txn:${txnId}')` with a nested `withLock('wallet:${txn.userId}')`. The eligibility test is a read-then-write: `const all = (await db.txn.listByStatus("AML_REVIEW")); const txn = all.find(t => t.id === txnId); if (!txn) return ...` (lines 146-148), keyed on the very status line 171 is responsible for changing. Reject requires ONE officer — the two-officer stage-1/stage-2 co-signature applies only to approve.
findings.whyItIsWrong: The comment above the lock, lines 142-144, states the guarantee: "Lock the whole reject on the transaction (like approveAmlAction) so two officers / a double-click can't both pass the AML_REVIEW check and refund twice — crediting the player's balance for the same withdrawal more than once." The lock delivers that for CONCURRENT clicks only. It does nothing for a SEQUENTIAL retry: if the credit commits and the status flip does not, the row is still AML_REVIEW, still in the officer's queue, and the second click passes every check and credits again. Ask the standing question of this guard — would it still pass if the feature were absent? Two clicks a minute apart are serialized by the lock either way; the lock is asserting a property (no double refund) that only the atomic status flip could provide, and the status flip is in a different commit.
findings.rulesReference: none - internal consistency (the guard's own stated contract at src/app/admin/aml/actions.ts:142-144)
findings.concreteScenario: A player withdraws exactly TZS 1,000,000, which trips the AML threshold (wallet-service.ts:1786 — `amlReason: "Threshold ≥ TZS 1,000,000"`). withdraw() Phase A has already moved balance -1,000,000 / hold +1,000,000. A compliance officer opens /admin/aml, types a reason and clicks Reject. Line 167 commits: balance +1,000,000, hold 0. The request then dies — a deploy restart, or line 171 throws and prisma-dal.ts:1383 swallows it to null (the return is not checked). The officer sees a failed/timed-out action, refreshes /admin/aml, and the transaction is STILL listed in AML_REVIEW. They click Reject again. Line 146's `listByStatus("AML_REVIEW")` finds it, line 151's self-review check passes (the officer is not the payee), and line 167 credits TZS 1,000,000 a second time. Wallet: balance +1,000,000 over, hold -1,000,000. walletReal is unchanged, so computeTrialBalance reports realDrift 0 and ok true.
findings.moneyImpact: TZS 1,000,000 handed to the player out of platform funds per retried reject — this path only ever handles amounts at or above the AML threshold, so every occurrence is at least seven figures. Undetectable by the nightly trial balance for the same balance+hold cancellation reason as MO-3.a. The retry is not a rare fault: an officer whose money-moving click appears to fail will click it again, and the queue still shows the row.

findings.title: Adjacent (initiation, same root): withdraw() Phase A also splits the debit from the Transaction row, and db.txn.create throws uncaught — stranding the gross in `hold` with no txn row that any sweep can find
findings.whatTheCodeDoes: Phase A debits the wallet at line 1630 — `const updated = await db.wallet.adjust(w.id, { balance: -amount, hold: amount }, { requireBalanceGte: amount });` — and creates the Transaction row at line 1638 — `await db.txn.create({ id: txnId, ... })`. Neither receives the lock's transaction client, so they are two independent auto-commits, and `prismaDb.txn.create` (prisma-dal.ts:1306-1330) has NO try/catch: a failure throws, escapes withLock (whose transaction contains nothing to roll back) and 500s the request. The `audit({ ... action: "withdraw.initiated" ... })` call is at line 1665, after the create, so it never runs either.
findings.whyItIsWrong: The code comment eight lines above already names this exact outcome as the thing to prevent (lines 1605-1611): "the second caller debits AGAIN and then db.txn.create throws on the @unique idempotencyKey — AFTER the debit — stranding funds in `hold` with no txn row (reconcileStalePayments scans txns, so it never finds/reverses them)." The fix that was applied is an in-lock idempotency re-check, which closes only the CONCURRENT-duplicate door. Every other cause of a create failure — a connection reset, a statement timeout, pool exhaustion, a redeploy SIGTERM between the two commits — leaves the identical wreckage the comment describes, and the comment reads as if the class were closed. This matters to this lane because it is the failure the refund path cannot repair: with no Transaction row there is nothing for `reconcileStalePayments` (which iterates `db.txn.listByStatus("PROCESSING")`, line 1228) to see, and `reverseStuckPayoutAction` needs a `txnId` (payment-actions.ts:241-248). There is no operator tool that can return that money.
findings.rulesReference: §2.8 — the player is charged the pool fee and the withdrawal fee and nothing else; losing the whole withdrawal to a stranded hold is a deduction that does not exist
findings.concreteScenario: Player has TZS 300,000 spendable and requests a TZS 250,000 withdrawal. Line 1630 commits: balance 50,000, hold 250,000. Line 1638's `transaction.create` errors on a transient DB fault (or the container is SIGTERMed between the two commits). The throw is not caught in prisma-dal, escapes withLock, and the player gets a 500. No Transaction row exists, no `withdraw.initiated` audit row exists. The player's wallet shows TZS 50,000 spendable where it showed TZS 300,000, and /wallet lists no transaction explaining the missing TZS 250,000. reconcileStalePayments never sees it (nothing PROCESSING), the fast payout lane never sees it (`db.txn.listByStatus("PROCESSING")`, line 1140), and /admin/payments has no row to act on. computeTrialBalance: walletReal = 50,000 + 250,000 = 300,000 = ledgerReal → realDrift 0, ok true.
findings.moneyImpact: TZS 250,000 of the player's own money is frozen indefinitely with no automated or operator route to release it, and no record that the request was ever made. Each occurrence needs a hand-written SQL correction against production. Undetectable by the trial balance for the same balance+hold reason as MO-3.d.

findings.title: The sweep's deposit safety arms are gated on isLiveMoneyMode() — an env switch that is still OFF on production — so 'we could not ask the gateway' auto-FAILS a genuinely paid deposit
findings.whatTheCodeDoes: Both deposit safety arms — "no providerRef" (line 1247) and "UNSUPPORTED, i.e. we could not read the provider's status" (line 1277) — are conditional on `isLiveMoneyMode()`. When that predicate is false the code falls through to `settleDepositFailed(t.id, "reconcile-timeout-no-ref")` / `settleDepositFailed(t.id, "reconcile-timeout")`, which marks the deposit FAILED (terminal, never revisited by any sweep) and emails the player "The payment was never started with your provider." or "The payment wasn't confirmed in time and has been cancelled." (friendlyFailureReason, lines 561-562).
findings.whyItIsWrong: `isLiveMoneyMode()` is `process.env.NODE_ENV === "production" && process.env.TEST_FUNDING !== "true"` (runtime-mode.ts:28-30) — it answers "has the go-live env switch been thrown?", NOT "is real cash moving through Selcom right now?". Those are different questions and on this deployment they disagree: whether real money moves is decided by the payment control plane (`getPaymentProvider()` resolving to `selcom`), which is entirely independent of TEST_FUNDING. docs/LIVE-HOSTING-STATUS.md:193 records `TEST_FUNDING=true` (pre-launch) as set on the live Railway service and line 34 lists the go-live switch as "⚪ Not started", while docs/SELCOM-DISBURSEMENT-ACTIVATION.md:165-166 records "Prod state (verified 2026-07-27, read-only): active provider = selcom (via PAYMENT_AGGREGATOR), gateway configured, money-mode = TEST (TEST_FUNDING on)." That is precisely the combination the comment says must never happen: the code's own words at lines 1273-1276 are "Terminalising on that is only safe when no real money can be in flight. In LIVE money mode a missing/So-broken credential would otherwise blind-FAIL genuinely paid deposits within one sweep" — and the predicate it chose says TEST while Selcom is live. The withdrawal arm was deliberately NOT mode-gated for exactly this reason (lines 1314-1316: "Gating it would leave a branch shaped exactly like the bug, waiting for someone to flip a flag"); the deposit arm still carries the flag.
findings.rulesReference: §2.8 — a player is charged the pool fee and the withdrawal fee and NOTHING ELSE. Taking a deposit and terminalising it as FAILED with no credit charges the player 100% of the deposit.
findings.concreteScenario: Production is NODE_ENV=production with TEST_FUNDING=true and the control plane set to selcom. A player deposits TZS 200,000 by M-Pesa at 10:00 and approves the USSD push; Selcom takes the money. A deploy drops or rotates PAYMENT_API_SECRET (or the control-plane hydration hits one transient DB error and pins the provider to the env fallback, as line 1310 describes). At 10:32 the sweep selects the deposit, `verifyDepositStatus` returns UNSUPPORTED because `selcomEnv()` is now null, `isLiveMoneyMode()` returns FALSE, so `settleDepositFailed(t.id, "reconcile-timeout")` fires: status FAILED, and the player is emailed "Deposit failed · TZS 200,000 — The payment wasn't confirmed in time and has been cancelled." FAILED is terminal, so no later sweep, webhook or return-page visit ever revisits it. Selcom still holds the 200,000.
findings.moneyImpact: The player loses the full deposit — 200,000 TZS in the example, repeated for EVERY in-flight deposit in the same sweep, since the condition is global rather than per-transaction. The player is also told in writing that no money was taken, which sends them to their bank to dispute rather than to support. Recovery requires manual reconciliation against Selcom's settlement file.

findings.title: An unparseable or field-renamed payout envelope resolves to FAILED, and FAILED is the one verdict that auto-refunds a payout that already left
findings.whatTheCodeDoes: `selcomFetch` reads the body as text and, on a parse failure, leaves `json = {}` (selcom.ts:339-341: `let json: SelcomEnvelope = {}; try { json = JSON.parse(rawBody) ... } catch { /* non-JSON body */ }`) while still returning `ok: res.ok`. `selcomVerifyPayout` returns null only for a transport error or `!res.ok`; anything with a 2xx goes to `envelopeSettlementVerdict`, where `code = String(json.resultcode ?? "").trim()` is `""` and `result` is `""`, neither matches the CONFIRMED test nor the non-terminal list, and control falls to the final `return "FAILED"`. That verdict reaches `reconcileStalePayments`, whose withdrawal arm is the ONE path that auto-reverses: `else if (v.status === "FAILED") { if (await settleWithdrawalFailed(t.id, "reconcile-verified-failed")) ... }` (wallet-service.ts:1304).
findings.whyItIsWrong: The identical question on the deposit side was deliberately answered the opposite way, and the reasoning is written into the file: `selcomVerifyOrder` ends `return { status: null }; // PENDING · INPROGRESS · empty · anything unknown → re-query`, above the comment "Anything unrecognised is treated as non-terminal too: waiting is recoverable, a wrong FAILED is not." On the payout side a wrong FAILED is strictly worse than on the deposit side — it does not merely delay a credit, it hands the player their money a second time — yet the payout mapper treats the ABSENCE of a result code as a definitive refusal. Selcom's documented codes justify "an unrecognised CODE is a fail"; they justify nothing about an envelope that carries no code at all. The exposure is not hypothetical field-drift: docs/SELCOM-API-DIGEST.md:107 records that Selcom's own callback body spells the field `resulcode /*sic — typo, no "t"*/`. If the wallet-cashin query envelope shares that spelling, or omits `result`, then `json.resultcode` is undefined for a SUCCESSFUL payout and this function returns FAILED for money that was paid. A 200 with an empty body, an HTML maintenance/WAF page, or a gzip/charset fault produces the same verdict.
findings.rulesReference: none - internal consistency: this contradicts the explicitly-documented rule in the same file (selcom.ts:848-854, "Non-terminal states must ALWAYS return null ... waiting is recoverable, a wrong FAILED is not") and the money-safety contract at wallet-service.ts:1008-1012.
findings.concreteScenario: Three players have withdrawals of TZS 1,000,000, 500,000 and 250,000 in PROCESSING, all dispatched and all genuinely paid by Selcom (net 985,000 / 492,500 / 246,250 delivered to their handsets). During a Selcom incident their edge returns HTTP 200 with an HTML interstitial instead of JSON — or the query envelope simply spells the field `resulcode`. Thirty minutes later `reconcileStalePayments` runs, `selcomVerifyPayout` gets `res.ok === true` with `json = {}` (or `{resulcode:'000'}`), `envelopeSettlementVerdict` returns FAILED for all three, and `settleWithdrawalFailed` credits 1,000,000 + 500,000 + 250,000 back to spendable balances and emails all three "Withdrawal returned". The providerStatus written to the row reads "FAILED: HTTP 200" — with no result code in it, which is itself the tell.
findings.moneyImpact: The house pays every affected in-flight payout twice: TZS 1,723,750 of delivered cash in this scenario, plus TZS 1,750,000 restored to wallets that the players can immediately withdraw again. It is systemic rather than per-player — one bad gateway response shape hits every PROCESSING withdrawal in the same sweep.

findings.title: The generic lane can settle a SELCOM transaction from the callback body — the session-1 fix keyed on the caller's self-declared provider, and no transaction records which gateway owns it
findings.whatTheCodeDoes: The session-1 fix refuses the generic lane only when the CALLER names selcom: `if (AUTHORITATIVE_ONLY.has(provider))` where `provider` is read straight from the caller's own `x-provider` header (line 82). It then verifies an HMAC with the secret for whichever provider the caller named, parses `reference` and `status` out of the body, and calls `settlePaymentWebhook({ providerRef: ref, status, amount })`. `settlePaymentWebhook` (wallet-service.ts:925-926) resolves the row with `db.txn.findByProviderRef(input.providerRef)` and never compares anything about the provider. It cannot: `StoredTxn.provider` is the MNO/rail — `"MPESA" | "TIGO_PESA" | "AIRTEL_MONEY" | "HALO_PESA" | "MIXX" | "TTCL_PESA" | "CARD" | "BANK_TRANSFER" | "INTERNAL" | null` (store.ts:268) — not the gateway, so there is no field that says a given `providerRef` belongs to Selcom rather than to Azampay or Mixx.
findings.whyItIsWrong: The header comment promises "Selcom now has exactly ONE door", but the door is bolted by NAME only. A caller holding `AZAMPAY_WEBHOOK_SECRET` or `MIXX_WEBHOOK_SECRET` — values shared with those vendors, and which `boot-checks.ts:46-56` actively nags an operator to set in production — sends `X-Provider: azampay` and a body naming a Selcom `providerRef`, and the transaction is settled from the body: no order-status re-query, no rail query, exactly the protections whose absence the session-1 note calls out ("Every protection on the Selcom money-in path lives in that handler"). The guard that is supposed to hold this line (`scripts/webhook-security.test.mts` §S.1-S.5) is a text match over the route file: it checks that the string `selcom` is absent from `KNOWN_PROVIDERS`, that the `if (AUTHORITATIVE_ONLY.has(provider))` line exists, and that the string `selcomVerifyOrder(env,` still appears. Every one of those assertions would still pass with the entire withdrawal branch deleted, and none of them observes that a transaction can be settled by a lane that does not own it. The red harness `webhook-money-red.mjs` mutates only the same two deposit-side strings.
findings.rulesReference: none - internal consistency: it defeats the stated invariant of this file's own header ("DEPOSITS are settled from an AUTHORITATIVE, signed order-status re-query") and RULES §2.8's guarantee about what a player is and is not charged.
findings.concreteScenario: A player initiates a TZS 1,000,000 deposit over Selcom mobile money and never approves the USSD prompt; the row sits PROCESSING with providerRef `dep_4c8f10ab22e1`, printed in full on their own wallet screen. Anyone with the Azampay integration secret (the vendor, an ex-integrator, anyone who has read the Railway variables) POSTs `X-Provider: azampay`, a fresh `X-Timestamp`, a valid `X-Signature`, and body `{"reference":"dep_4c8f10ab22e1","status":"COMPLETED","amount":1000000}`. `AUTHORITATIVE_ONLY` does not fire (the header says azampay), the signature validates against `AZAMPAY_WEBHOOK_SECRET`, the M4 amount check passes because 1,000,000 equals the initiated amount, and `settleDepositConfirmed` credits TZS 1,000,000 that no player ever paid. The same request with `"status":"FAILED"` against a live Selcom withdrawal's `wdr_…` reference refunds a payout that already left.
findings.moneyImpact: Uncapped credit of money never received (up to the initiated amount, repeatable with a fresh unpaid deposit each time), or a double-paid withdrawal. TZS 1,000,000 per request in the scenario above, limited only by how many deposits the attacker initiates.

findings.title: CARD has no kill-switch: MNOS is derived from MOBILE_MONEY_METHODS, so isPaymentPaused("CARD",…) can never be true on the only rail carrying chargeback risk
findings.whatTheCodeDoes: `isPaymentPaused(provider, kind)` answers `!!kstore[provider]?.[kind]`. `kstore` has exactly two writers: `Object.assign(kstore, stored)` in `ensureKill()` (hydrating SystemConfig["payments.killswitch"]) and `setKillSwitch(provider: Mno, …)`. `Mno = MobileMoneyMethodId = "MPESA"|"AIRTEL_MONEY"|"HALO_PESA"|"MIXX"`, and `MNOS` is `MOBILE_MONEY_METHODS.map(...)`, i.e. the four rails with `mobileMoney: true` in `PAYMENT_METHODS`. CARD is `mobileMoney: false` (payment-providers.ts:98) so it is not in MNOS. The only caller of `setKillSwitch` is `toggleKillSwitchAction`, which additionally refuses anything not in MNOS (`if (!MNOS.some((m) => m.id === provider)) return { ok: false, error: "Unknown provider." }`, payment-actions.ts:45). `getKillSwitches()` enumerates MNOS only, so /admin/payments renders exactly four health cards, each with a `<KillSwitch>` — and no Card card at all (page.tsx:226–283). Meanwhile the deposit money path calls the switch with whatever the schema accepted: `if (await isPaymentPaused(parse.data.provider, "deposits"))` (wallet-service.ts:107), and `DepositSchema.provider` is `z.enum(["MPESA","AIRTEL_MONEY","HALO_PESA","MIXX","CARD"])` (validators.ts:180). /wallet/deposit ships a live `{ id: "CARD", name: "Card", hue: 200 }` tile with no `unavailable` flag (deposit/page.tsx:46, 188), and `selcomAdapter.deposit` has a real hosted-checkout branch for it (payments.ts:333).
findings.whyItIsWrong: No code path can ever put a `CARD` key into the kill-switch map, and no admin surface offers one, so the emergency STOP is structurally unreachable for card deposits. Card is the one rail on 50pick that carries chargeback risk — Tanzanian mobile money has no chargeback — so the rail that most needs an emergency stop is the only money-in rail that has none. The page header even reads "MNO health · 24h window", and the four toggles read as the complete set: an officer in an incident pauses all four MNOs, which stops legitimate mobile money and does not stop cards. The only lever that does stop card deposits is the platform-wide `isMaintenanceMode()` (wallet-service.ts:84), which also stops every other deposit AND all new bets — a whole-platform outage as the only response to a single-rail incident. `scripts/payment-killswitch.test.mts` never names CARD (it drives MPESA and AIRTEL only), so it would pass byte-identically if card deposits did not exist — it cannot fail on this.
findings.rulesReference: none - internal consistency (RULES.md does not legislate the kill-switch; docs/MONEY-GATE-REMEDIATION.md §3.2 names this lead as UNVERIFIED — this lane confirms it)
findings.concreteScenario: A card-fraud ring runs 40 CARD deposits of TZS 250,000 each through /wallet/deposit (each inside the deposit bounds; the stake bounds 1,000…1,000,000 bind the bets that follow). TZS 10,000,000 is credited. The players stake and then withdraw on MPESA, which is a different rail and is not paused. An officer spots the pattern and opens /admin/payments: four toggles — M-Pesa, Airtel Money, HaloPesa, Mixx by Yas. They pause all four. `isPaymentPaused("CARD", "deposits")` still evaluates `!!kstore["CARD"]?.deposits` → `kstore["CARD"]` is `undefined` → `false`. Card deposits keep landing. The only stop available is platform-wide maintenance mode, which also halts every legitimate M-Pesa deposit and every new bet on both products.
findings.moneyImpact: The platform carries the full chargeback exposure of every card deposit taken after the incident is detected, with no per-rail way to stop it. In the scenario above that is TZS 10,000,000 charged back with the cash already withdrawn on a rail with no reversal. The alternative — maintenance mode — costs all deposit and all betting revenue platform-wide for the duration.

findings.title: reconcileWriteOffAction stamps a per-OFFICER sentinel, not a per-transaction one — the second write-off collides on @@unique([provider, providerRef]), the DAL swallows the error, and the action still returns ok:true and writes a COMPLIANCE "written_off" audit row
findings.whatTheCodeDoes: The write-off stamps `providerRef: `WRITEOFF-${g.userId.slice(0, 10)}`` — a string derived only from the officer's id, identical for every row that officer ever writes off. `Transaction` carries `@@unique([provider, providerRef])` (schema.prisma:621). `db.txn.update` in the Prisma DAL is `try { return await run(); } catch { return null; }` when no outer transaction is passed (prisma-dal.ts:1383), so a P2002 unique violation is swallowed and returns `null`. `reconcileWriteOffAction` never reads the return value: it `await`s the update, then unconditionally writes `audit({ category: "COMPLIANCE", action: "payments.reconcile.written_off", … payload: { reason, type: t.type, amount: Math.abs(t.amount) } })`, revalidates, and returns `{ ok: true }`. The client (`reconcile-controls.tsx:65`) fires `deferToast({ title: "Written off", variant: "success" })` on `r.ok`. The same call also overwrites `amlReason` with the write-off text, clobbering any AML-review rationale the row carried.
findings.whyItIsWrong: A write-off is a money decision on a licensed platform. On the second write-off by the same officer against the same rail, nothing is written to the row, the transaction keeps `providerRef = null` and stays in the drift list — but the officer is told it succeeded and a COMPLIANCE audit row now asserts that a specific amount was written off when the database says otherwise. That is a regulator-facing record that is false, produced by a green success path. It is invisible to any suite that runs against the in-memory store: `store.ts:1164-1170` `update` is a plain `Map.set` with no unique constraint at all, so the collision can only ever fire against Postgres. There is no test anywhere in `scripts/` that exercises `reconcileWriteOffAction`.
findings.rulesReference: none - internal consistency (RULES.md §5 step 6 — "verify by reading the database"; the audit record and the database disagree here)
findings.concreteScenario: Officer `usr_k3n8x9qa77` opens /admin/payments. Two unmatched CONFIRMED movements are listed, both on M-Pesa: a deposit of TZS 120,000 and a withdrawal of TZS 400,000, neither carrying a PSP ref. They write off the deposit with reason "manual float top-up, no Selcom leg" — the row gets `providerRef = "WRITEOFF-usr_k3n8x"`. They then write off the withdrawal with reason "internal correction". Postgres refuses: `(provider=MPESA, providerRef='WRITEOFF-usr_k3n8x')` already exists. `db.txn.update` catches it and returns null. The action returns `{ ok: true }`; the modal shows the green "Written off" toast; a COMPLIANCE audit row records `payments.reconcile.written_off · amount 400,000`. The TZS 400,000 withdrawal still has `providerRef = null`, still counts in `reconcile().unmatched`, and still adds TZS 400,000 to the drift figure the officer was trying to clear.
findings.moneyImpact: No shillings move — but the compliance record of a TZS 400,000 write-off is fabricated, and the unmatched item it claims to have cleared is still outstanding. An officer who trusts the toast stops chasing a real TZS 400,000 reconciliation gap; an auditor reading the COMPLIANCE log counts a write-off decision that never touched the ledger. Every write-off after an officer's first on a given rail is affected, indefinitely.

findings.title: reverseStuckPayoutAction skips the provider re-query entirely when providerRef is null, while the modal promises the provider is asked — and the guard that "proves" the re-query is a regex over the source that cannot see the conditional
findings.whatTheCodeDoes: The doc-block states unconditionally: "before reversing we RE-QUERY the provider, and refuse outright if it reports CONFIRMED. Reversing a payout that actually settled would pay the player twice." The code puts the whole machine check inside `if (t.providerRef) { … }`. With no ref, `providerSays` stays the literal string `"not asked (no provider reference)"`, no `verifyWithdrawalStatus` call is made, and execution falls straight through to `settleWithdrawalFailed(txnId, "officer-reversed-stuck-payout")`, which refunds the hold to spendable balance and marks the row FAILED. The officer's modal says, without qualification: "The provider is asked one more time. If it reports the payout completed, this is refused — reversing a payout that actually settled would pay the player twice." (stuck-payout-controls.tsx:96-99). A PROCESSING withdrawal with `providerRef = null` is reachable: `withdraw()` creates the row with `providerRef: null`, dispatches over the network, and only then writes the ref via `db.txn.update` — which swallows any DB error into `null` (prisma-dal.ts:1383) and is not retried; a crash or redeploy in that window leaves the same state permanently. Such a row appears in the frozen-payouts alarm list after 30 minutes, rendered as "no provider response recorded" (page.tsx:147), with the "Return to player" button beside it.
findings.whyItIsWrong: The one control described as "the last thing standing between an officer and a double payment" is silently absent for exactly the population it exists for. Worse, the repo's own automated sweep takes the opposite decision on the identical state: `reconcileStalePayments` refuses to touch a stale withdrawal with no ref — `if (!ref) { leftPending++; auditNeedsReviewOnce(t.id, "stale withdrawal has no providerRef — not auto-reversed", {}); continue; }` (wallet-service.ts:1290) — so the machine is more careful than the officer action, and the officer is told the opposite of what the code does. The guard that claims to prove this is `scripts/payout-observability.test.mts:141-143`, a regex over the source text: `/verifyWithdrawalStatus[\s\S]{0,400}if \(v\.status === "CONFIRMED"\)[\s\S]{0,700}return \{ ok: false/.test(reverseFn)`. It matches characters, not control flow — it passes unchanged whether the block is conditional or not, and would still pass if the whole `if (t.providerRef)` wrapper made the query unreachable.
findings.rulesReference: none - internal consistency (the code's own doc-block and the officer-facing modal both state a check the code does not always perform)
findings.concreteScenario: A player withdraws TZS 500,000 on M-Pesa. `withdraw()` places the hold and creates the row PROCESSING with `providerRef: null`, then `dispatchWithdrawal` succeeds and Selcom queues the payout. The post-dispatch `db.txn.update(txnId, { providerRef: result.providerRef, … })` hits a transient Postgres error; `db.txn.update` catches it and returns null; nothing retries. Thirty-one minutes later the row appears on /admin/payments under "Frozen payouts · 1", showing "500,000 · …held 31m" and "no provider response recorded". An officer clicks "Return to player", reads "The provider is asked one more time. If it reports the payout completed, this is refused", types "Selcom 403 — payout never dispatched", and confirms. Because `t.providerRef` is null, Selcom is never asked. `settleWithdrawalFailed` returns TZS 500,000 to the player's spendable balance and emails them "Withdrawal returned · TZS 500,000". Selcom then delivers the original TZS 500,000 to the same handset.
findings.moneyImpact: TZS 500,000 paid twice on a single withdrawal request — once by Selcom out of the disbursement float, once back into the player's spendable balance where they can stake or withdraw it again. The platform absorbs the whole TZS 500,000. The COMPLIANCE audit row records `providerSays: "not asked (no provider reference)"`, so the loss is at least traceable afterwards, but nothing prevented it and the officer was told a check had run.

findings.title: setKillSwitch reports the emergency STOP applied before it is durable — the persist is `void saveConfig(...)` and saveConfig never throws, so a failed write leaves the pause in one process's memory with the officer told it succeeded
findings.whatTheCodeDoes: `setKillSwitch` mutates the in-process `kstore`, then fires `void saveConfig(KILL_KEY, kstore)` — not awaited, return value discarded. `saveConfig` is documented as "No-op without a DB; never throws" and its body is `try { await client.systemConfig.upsert(...) } catch (err) { console.error(...) }` (config-store.ts:53-68), so a write failure produces a log line and nothing else. It also no-ops entirely when `hasDatabase()` is false or `prisma()` returns null. `setKillSwitch` returns `Promise<void>` with no result, and `toggleKillSwitchAction` returns `{ ok: true }` unconditionally after awaiting it, and the COMPLIANCE audit `payments.killswitch.paused` is written regardless.
findings.whyItIsWrong: This is the write-side twin of the blocker MONEY-GATE-REMEDIATION §1.2 already fixed on the read side. That fix stopped one failed read from pinning a container on "nothing is paused" for its whole life; it did not make the write durable or observable. The kill-switch is the emergency STOP on the money-in and money-out paths, and the officer's confirmation that it is in force is unconditional — it cannot fail, so it cannot tell the truth. Railway's deploy configuration for this service is `numReplicas 1` with `overlapSeconds` and `drainingSeconds` both null (RAILWAY-LIVE.md:100-104), so "any restart is a full outage" and every deploy is a fresh process that re-hydrates `kstore` from SystemConfig only. If the upsert failed, the pause is gone at the next deploy with no signal anywhere except a rotated container log.
findings.rulesReference: none - internal consistency (docs/MONEY-GATE-REMEDIATION.md §1.2 records the read-side half of this as a fixed blocker; the write side is untouched)
findings.concreteScenario: An M-Pesa fraud pattern is spotted. The officer opens /admin/payments and toggles M-Pesa deposits to PAUSED. `kstore.MPESA.deposits = true` in the serving process; the toggle renders claret "PAUSED BY usr_k3n8x9 · 09 Sep 2026 14:02"; a COMPLIANCE audit row is written. The `systemConfig.upsert` fails — pool exhaustion during the incident's own traffic spike, or a Postgres failover. `saveConfig` logs `[config] save "payments.killswitch" failed:` and returns; `setKillSwitch` returns void; the action returns ok. Ninety minutes later a routine deploy restarts the single replica. The new process hydrates `payments.killswitch` from SystemConfig, which still holds the pre-incident map. `isPaymentPaused("MPESA", "deposits")` is false again. M-Pesa deposits resume. /admin/payments now renders M-Pesa as "Live · malipo", and nobody was told anything changed.
findings.moneyImpact: The emergency stop on a live fraud incident silently lifts itself at the next deploy. Every fraudulent M-Pesa deposit taken after that point — TZS 250,000 each in the pattern above — lands on a rail the officer believes is closed, and the console agrees with the officer that it was closed until the moment it re-renders as Live. The same applies to withdrawals: a paused payout rail resumes dispatching real money out.

findings.title: repairOrphanedPositions refunds real money to a wallet with NO ledger entry at all, and leaves POOL:{marketId} holding the stake for a market that no longer exists
findings.whatTheCodeDoes: The whole function (lines 2554-2619) walks every OPEN position whose market row is gone, credits the real part of the stake straight onto the wallet with `db.wallet.adjust(w.id, { balance: realRefund })`, returns the bonus part via `refundBonusToActive` (which also writes no ledger entry), marks the position VOID, writes a CONFIRMED BET_REFUND Transaction row and an audit row. There is no `postLedgerEntries` call, no `refundEntries` call and no `withMoneyTx` anywhere in the function — `market-service.ts` imports `refundEntries` and uses it at lines 3342, 3471 and 4148, but not here.
findings.whyItIsWrong: At bet time `stakeEntries` posted PLAYER:{userId} −stake / POOL:{marketId} +stake. The orphan repair moves the money back into the wallet without posting the mirror. The double-entry record therefore says the player is still down the stake and the pool of a deleted market still holds it. This is the exact failure the lane brief names: the books sum to zero perfectly (nothing was written, so nothing can be imbalanced) while a suspense account holds money for an object that no longer exists. `reconcileLedger` is structurally blind to it — ledger.ts's own comment at line ~693 says so: "structurally blind to a group that was NEVER WRITTEN". The only detector is the nightly `trialBalance`, which reports it as unattributed per-wallet drift with no group, no memo and no txnId to explain it.
findings.rulesReference: none - internal consistency. The invariant is ledger.ts's own contract: "Every money movement is recorded as a balanced group of entries where SUM(amount) = 0 within each groupId" (ledger.ts:4-6) and `withMoneyTx`'s "its wallet mutation, its Transaction row, and its ledger entries commit ATOMICALLY (audit C3)" (ledger.ts:31-33). RULES.md §6a explicitly records that the `money-out` audit lane never ran.
findings.concreteScenario: Player P holds one OPEN position with a real stake of TZS 500,000 on market M (inside the §2.3 bounds of 1,000…1,000,000). Bet time booked PLAYER:P −500,000 and POOL:M +500,000. M's PredictionMarket row is later removed — `marketStore.delete(m.id)` at market-service.ts:4279 is a real `predictionMarket.delete` (market-dal.ts:963), and this function's own caller comment at market-service.ts:4286-4287 says it exists to "Sweep orphaned positions left over from the deletion bug that Sprint 56.4 fixed". On the next boot (lifecycle.ts:474 runs it on EVERY boot, so on every deploy) the wallet is credited 500,000 at line 2586 and a CONFIRMED BET_REFUND Transaction is written at line 2593. Outcome: P's wallet is TZS 500,000 higher than Σ PLAYER:P in the ledger; POOL:M still carries +500,000 for a market row that does not exist; `reconcileLedger()` returns `imbalanced: []`; `SELECT SUM(amount) FROM LedgerEntry` is still exactly 0.
findings.moneyImpact: TZS 500,000 of real, withdrawable money leaves the house with no double-entry record of it leaving. The house book's per-game identity for M closes to +500,000 instead of 0 (`gameBook.closesTo = handle − paidOut − bonusRefunded − feeBooked`, house-book.ts:258 — paidOut is 0 because no REFUND row was written), so the owner is shown a phantom 500,000 of retained pool. The nightly trial balance carries a permanent, unexplainable +500,000 realDrift on that wallet which then MASKS any later genuine drift on the same wallet. Repeats once per orphaned position, unbounded.

findings.title: HOUSE:TAX is credited again by the live agent programme but is excluded from `owedToOthers`, so the solvency line reports tax owed to TRA as the owner's free cash — and both admin pages label the account "RETIRED"
findings.whatTheCodeDoes: `housePosition` computes `const owedToOthers = leviesPayable + aggregator + rgSuspense;` and then `freeHouseCash: input.custodialCash - input.playerLiability - owedToOthers`. `HouseAccounts` names only commission, agentCommission, traLevy, gbtLevy, aggregator and rgSuspense; HOUSE:TAX arrives only inside the untyped `all` map, which is used for rendering and nothing else. Meanwhile `agentCommissionEntries` (ledger.ts:584) credits `acct.tax` = "HOUSE:TAX" with the 5% agent withholding, and `agentRegistrationFeeEntries` (ledger.ts:624) credits it with the 18% registration-fee VAT. Nothing anywhere debits HOUSE:TAX except the registration-fee refund mirror.
findings.whyItIsWrong: HOUSE:TAX now holds two live, statutory liabilities — VAT collected from an applicant and withholding tax deducted from an agent's income — both owed to TRA. RULES §2.10 states the withholding is "remitted to `HOUSE:TAX` in the same balanced ledger group as the credit" and the registration VAT "posts to `HOUSE:AGENT_FEE` (net) + `HOUSE:TAX` (VAT)". The solvency line's whole stated purpose (house-book.ts:113-117: "Every claim on the cash is subtracted here, explicitly, so no caller can present a gross figure as the owner's money") is defeated for this one account, and /admin/house's "How the position is derived" table (page.tsx:485-489) enumerates exactly four claim lines and has none for it. Worse, both consoles actively tell the officer the balance is dead: `"HOUSE:TAX": "RETIRED — historical rows only"` at src/app/admin/house/page.tsx:69 and src/app/admin/finance/page.tsx:46. The one guard that touches HOUSE:TAX — scripts/house-book.test.mts:187-194, assertion "3c.4" — is vacuous: it evaluates `Object.keys(housePosition({...}) && { ok: 1 }).length === 1`, i.e. `Object.keys({ok:1}).length === 1`, which is true regardless of what `housePosition` does with `all` or with HOUSE:TAX. It would still pass if the field were deleted.
findings.rulesReference: RULES.md §2.10 ("Withholding … remitted to `HOUSE:TAX` in the same balanced ledger group as the credit"; "Registration fee … It never enters the player ledger; it posts to `HOUSE:AGENT_FEE` (net) + `HOUSE:TAX` (VAT)") and §2.2 (taxes are the state's, never the owner's).
findings.concreteScenario: Two applicants are approved onto the live agent programme. Each pays the TZS 118,000 registration fee (§2.10: 100,000 net + 18,000 VAT, EXCLUSIVE since 2026-09-08) and an officer runs `reconcileFee` (agent-application-service.ts:745). Each posts EXTERNAL:SELCOM −118,000 / HOUSE:AGENT_FEE +100,000 / HOUSE:TAX +18,000. `readCustodialCash` now reports railBacked TZS 236,000 higher; `readHouseAccounts` reports HOUSE:TAX = 36,000. Because `owedToOthers` does not contain it, `freeHouseCash` rises by the full 236,000 when only 200,000 is the owner's. Then one of those agents earns commission: a poll where ten players each staked TZS 100,000 on the losing side gives a losing pool of 1,000,000, a §2.1 fee of 130,000, `levySplit` → TRA 13,000 + GBT 6,500, operatorNet 110,500; at the live 10% rate the gross commission is 11,050 and `splitWithholding` withholds 5% = 553 to HOUSE:TAX. HOUSE:TAX = 36,553, none of it subtracted.
findings.moneyImpact: The owner's solvency line on /admin/house overstates free house cash by exactly Σ HOUSE:TAX — TZS 36,553 in the scenario above, growing by 18,000 per collected registration fee and by 5% of every agent commission accrual, forever, because nothing ever debits the account. The officer reading the account panel beside it is told the growing balance is "RETIRED — historical rows only", so the misstatement is actively signposted as not-money. Repeatable on every agent and every accrual; the statutory pack read off HOUSE:TAX is the same figure the console calls retired.

findings.title: The withdrawal minimum has three homes; every player-facing one says 1,000 and the only enforced one is 1,016
findings.whatTheCodeDoes:
THE THREE HOMES, found and named.

HOME 1 — `WITHDRAW_MIN_TZS = 1_000` (src/lib/server/validators.ts:87). It is the zod message at validators.ts:100, the server-action bound at withdraw/actions.ts:95, the client-side confirm guard at withdraw-confirm.tsx:85, and the figure rendered in the wallet Limits tab (wallet/page.tsx:328 -> wallet-client.tsx:658 `capStr(limits.withdrawMin, limits.withdrawMax)` -> "TZS 1,000 – 5,000,000").

HOME 2 — the copy: `t.wallet.amountHint` = "Min TZS 1,000 · Max TZS 5,000,000 per withdrawal…", hardcoded in all three languages (i18n-dict.ts:1104 EN, :3369 SW, :5423 ZH). It is the field hint under the amount box (page.tsx:204), the toast a player gets when the client guard refuses (withdraw-confirm.tsx:86, :101), AND the sentence the server action echoes on its own bound refusal (actions.ts:96).

HOME 3 — `minWithdrawalForRate(rate)` (payout.ts:549). It reaches the client once, at page.tsx:209, as an HTML `min` attribute (which is inert — see MO-9.g), and it is the ONLY minimum actually enforced, at wallet-service.ts:1580.

COMPUTED BY HAND at the live 1.5%: `Math.ceil(1000 / (1 - 0.015))` = `Math.ceil(1000 / 0.985)` = `Math.ceil(1015.2284…)` = **1016**.

So the enforced floor is 1,016 and every number the player can read says 1,000.
findings.whyItIsWrong: RULES §2.9 requires every player-facing refusal to state the reason and the NEXT STEP. Here the screen states a bound it does not enforce, the two-step money-commit dialog quotes a net the platform cannot send, and the refusal that finally arrives names a figure that contradicts the hint 20px above it — and, for a small balance, a figure the player cannot reach. The whole point of the derived minimum (payout.ts:537-548: "a constant '1,016' would silently break the day someone edits the fee, in exactly the way that is invisible until a player is refused") is defeated by the copy and the Limits tab hardcoding 1,000 anyway.
findings.rulesReference: §2.9 (a refusal states the reason and the next step); §2.7 (the fee, and the derived floor that follows from it)
findings.concreteScenario: A player holds exactly TZS 1,010 (cash balance, no bonus, no hold). /wallet/withdraw shows "Available TZS 1,010". The hint under the amount box reads "Min TZS 1,000 · Max TZS 5,000,000 per withdrawal". The Limits tab on /wallet reads "Per withdrawal · TZS 1,000 – 5,000,000". Every quick-amount chip is filtered out (WITHDRAW_QUICK starts at 5,000, AmountField line 44 drops chips above `max`). The player types 1010. `WithdrawConfirm.validate()` passes (1010 >= 1000). The confirm dialog opens and states, in gold, the loudest line on the screen: "Amount TZS 1,010 · Withdrawal fee −TZS 15 · You receive TZS 995". The player taps "Send funds". `withdrawAction` passes (1010 >= WITHDRAW_MIN_TZS). `withdraw()` computes fee = round(1010 × 0.015) = 15, net = 995, and 995 < PROVIDER_MIN_PAYOUT_TZS(1000), so it refuses with `withdraw_below_min`, detail {net: 1000, min: 1016}. The player is redirected back and reads, under the red headline "Withdrawal didn't go through": "The smallest amount we can send after the fee is TZS 1,000. Withdraw at least TZS 1,016." — an instruction they cannot follow with a 1,010 balance, on the same screen whose hint still says the minimum is TZS 1,000. Same sequence at exactly the advertised minimum: enter 1,000, be promised "You receive TZS 985", be refused one tap later.
findings.moneyImpact: TZS 1,010 (and any balance in the band 1,000…1,014) is unwithdrawable while every displayed limit says it is above the minimum. The player's only route out is to DEPOSIT more money in order to withdraw money — a step no screen names. No shillings are misrouted; the loss is stranded balance plus a money-commit dialog that promises a net (TZS 995 / TZS 985) the platform will not pay. Repeats for every account in that band, forever, until the copy is fixed.

findings.title: /wallet/withdraw renders arbitrary ?error= query text in a first-party alert box, and the ratchet that swears this channel is at zero cannot see it
findings.whatTheCodeDoes:
page.tsx:60 reads `sp.error`, decodes it, and page.tsx:152-159 renders it verbatim inside a `role="alert"` box under the bold headline "Withdrawal didn't go through". Nothing validates the value against the failure registry. The same pattern is on /wallet/deposit (deposit/page.tsx:63 and :131).

RULES §2.9 records this channel as CLOSED: "All five such surfaces used to put the server's English sentence on the query string and render {sp.error} as text. They now carry the reason KEY … An unrecognised `?reason=` now renders nothing at all." Grepping `bannerFor`/`reasonKeyFor` finds exactly five call sites — auth/reset-password, profile/account, profile/kyc, profile/responsible-gambling, profile/source-of-funds. The two WALLET surfaces were never converted.

And the guard that reports the channel at zero is blind by construction. scripts/feedback-law.test.mts:412 matches the literal JSX `{sp.error}`. The withdraw page assigns to a local first and renders `{errorMsg}`, so the regex finds nothing. A repo-wide grep for `{sp.error}` in non-admin .tsx returns 0 — which is precisely why `CEILING = 0` (line 449) passes. Its own positive control (8.0a) tests a synthetic string literal, not the tree, so it passes whether or not the scanner can see the real files. Asked the standing question — "would this still pass if the feature were absent?" — the answer is yes.

findings.title: The settlement residual is NOT kept by the house — exactly 1 TZS is stranded in POOL:<marketId> whenever the fee has a fractional part, and test:pool-residual cannot see it because its fixture pre-rounds the fee that settlement does not round
findings.whatTheCodeDoes: poolFee returns an UNROUNDED fee and netPool: under loser-share `const fee = loserRate * losingPool;` and `netPool: pool - fee` (payout.ts:477, 483); under capped-commission `const fee = Math.min(commission, ceiling);` where `ceiling = r.feeCeilingRate * smaller` (payout.ts:492-493). settleMarket passes those raw floats straight to the two allocators (market-service.ts, `allocateWinnerPayouts(..., winningPool, settleFee.netPool)` and `allocateFeeShares(..., winningPool, settleFee.fee)`). allocateWinnerPayouts distributes exactly `Math.floor(netPool)`; allocateFeeShares distributes exactly `Math.max(0, Math.floor(fee))`. The ledger then debits POOL:<marketId> `payout + commAmt` per winner and nothing else (ledger.ts:372-375), while every bet credited POOL the full integer stake (ledger.ts:296).
findings.whyItIsWrong: Let G be the integer gross pool and F the real fee. The pool gives up floor(G - F) + floor(F). When F is an integer that is exactly G. When F has any fractional part, floor(G - F) = G - floor(F) - 1, so the pool gives up G - 1 and **1 whole shilling is left in POOL:<marketId> forever** — not a sub-shilling, and not with the house. payout.ts's own docblock claims otherwise, and pool-residual.test.mts's title states the invariant this breaks: 'a settled market's escrow account must hold EXACTLY nothing'. Nothing sweeps it: grep for a residual/escrow sweep across src returns no such job. The guard cannot object because its fixture builds a fee that can never be fractional — `const fee = Math.round(feeRate * loserPool);` — a line settlement does not have. Its own most adversarial case, `check("seven odd winners", …, 3331)`, is precisely the one that would have caught this: the guard computes fee 433 and residual 0, while real settlement computes fee 433.03 and residual 1. Would the guard still pass if the fix were absent? Yes — it is passing over this today, and the RED harness only proves it catches the different, 2026-08-11 Math.round-commission defect.
findings.rulesReference: none - internal consistency: payout.ts:679-680's claim vs the ledger, and pool-residual.test.mts's stated invariant. RULES.md §1 records 'residual 0.00' on both real settlements as a property of the model, so a systematically non-zero residual contradicts the law's own production evidence.
findings.concreteScenario: Long-form poll frozen at loser-share 13%. Player A stakes TZS 10,000 on YES; Player B stakes TZS 1,050 on NO (a whole number inside 1,000…1,000,000, accepted by buyPosition's `!Number.isInteger(opts.stake)` check). YES wins. losingPool = 1,050, fee = 0.13 x 1,050 = 136.5, gross = 11,050, netPool = 10,913.5. allocateWinnerPayouts pays A floor(10,913.5) = TZS 10,913; allocateFeeShares books floor(136.5) = TZS 136 to HOUSE:COMMISSION. POOL:<marketId> was credited 11,050 and gives up 10,913 + 136 = 11,049 — **TZS 1 stranded in escrow for a market that is finished**. Verified numerically against the allocators' exact algorithm: {gross 11050, fee 136.5, paid 10913, comm 136, residual 1}. The guard's own 'seven odd winners' shape (stakes 1,000/1,137/1,274/1,411/1,548/1,685/1,822 against a losing pool of 3,331) gives {gross 13208, fee 433.03, paid 12774, comm 433, residual 1} in production and residual 0 in the guard.
findings.moneyImpact: TZS 1 per settlement, borne by the house (it books 136 where 136.5 was owed) and stranded in a suspense account rather than kept. Small in isolation; the real cost is that it turns the platform's own escrow-closes-at-zero signal into noise. That signal is exactly what surfaced the 2026-08-11 defect (9 pools non-zero, 7 negative, net -6 TZS) — once every fractional-fee settlement leaves +1 behind, a genuine -1 or +5 is indistinguishable from routine dust. RULES.md §1's proud 'residual 0.00' is true only because both audited settlements had losing pools of 14,000 and 13,000, i.e. multiples of 100, where 13% is exactly integral.

findings.title: The winner-floor guardrail's predicate is an identity under loser-share, so the save-time refusal and the two console surfaces that quote it are constant-true instruments that affirm safety at a 100% take
findings.whatTheCodeDoes: Under loser-share, poolFee returns netPool = pool − loserRate × losingPool with loserRate clamped to [0, 1]. Therefore netPool >= pool − losingPool = winningPool for every possible rate, and worstCaseWinnerRatio's `netPool / winningPool` is >= 1 identically. `worst.ratio < 1` is unsatisfiable. I swept all 5,151 savable (platformFeeRate, operatorFeeRate) hundredth-percent pairs: the minimum ratio the guardrail can ever compute is exactly 1.000 (at 0% + 100%). Out-of-range rates (5.0 + 5.0) and NaN both also return >= 1 because of the same clamp.
findings.whyItIsWrong: Apply the standard question — would this check still pass if the feature were absent? Yes: delete the entire loser-share validation block and the guardrail still returns ok for every rate pair, because its question ("is a winner paid at least his stake?") is answered by the model's structure, not by the rates. It can only ever object to capped-commission configs. Worse, two officer-facing surfaces present that tautology as a live safety reading: /admin/config's "Worst winner ratio" KPI renders 1.000× with the green up-delta "never below 1.00× — a correct call cannot lose", and the simulator's brand-toned callout is titled "A correct call cannot lose money". At a 100% take both are literally true and completely misleading — the winner does not lose money, he wins nothing.
findings.rulesReference: none — internal consistency. The claim that the guardrail is "wired to feeCeilingRate" is FALSE (see clearedClaims); it is model-aware and still structurally unable to object.
findings.concreteScenario: After the LEAD-D.a save (Platform 50 + Operator 50), an officer reloads /admin/config to check the change. worstCaseWinnerRatio(config) returns ratio = 1.000, so the KPI renders "1.000×" with deltaDir "up" and the caption "never below 1.00× — a correct call cannot lose". Opening the fee simulator with the default YES 300,000 / NO 10,500 and stake 100,000 on YES: fee = 10,500, netPool = 300,000, payout = round((100,000/300,000) × 300,000) = TZS 100,000, ratio 1.000, so the danger branch (`sim.res.ratio < 1`) is not taken and the officer reads the brand callout "A correct call cannot lose money — This stake gets back TZS 100,000 on TZS 100,000 staked (1.000×)… the worst any winner can do is 1.000× — never below 1.000×." Three green affirmations on the screen whose stated purpose is "see what a rate actually does to a real player, before saving it" (fee-simulator.tsx:4).
findings.moneyImpact: No shillings move because of this finding on its own; it is what lets LEAD-D.a stand unnoticed. On the 300,000/10,500 book above, the house takes the entire TZS 10,500 losing pool and every YES holder is paid exactly stake — a TZS 100,000 position earns TZS 0 where the rule's 13% would earn TZS 455 — while the console reports the configuration as safe.

findings.title: Both guards that look like they police the house's share run only on the retired capped-commission knob — the suite pins feeModel to capped-commission at line 89, and the caption suite treats 100% as the normal maximum an operator may configure
findings.whatTheCodeDoes: scripts/fee-model.test.mts is the suite named in RULES §2.1 as a guard for the fee rule. Line 89 pins the whole suite: `await setGlobalConfig({ feeModel: "capped-commission" }, "fee-model-test-setup")`. Its §10, headed "THE GUARDRAIL — admin cannot save a config that could underpay a winner", exercises only feeCeilingRate (1.4 refused, 0.8 warned) and never sets platformFeeRate or operatorFeeRate. Its §7 asserts "we never take more than a third of the prize" against `DEFAULT_FEE_CEILING_RATE` using RATES, which carries no feeModel and therefore resolves to capped-commission (readRates, payout.ts:363). scripts/loser-share-fee.test.mts contains no rate-ceiling assertion at all. No test file in the repo references MAX_LOSER_SHARE_RATE except the caption suite, and that one asserts the clamp is displayed, not that a high rate is refused.
findings.whyItIsWrong: Would either guard still pass if the feature were absent? Yes. Delete market-config.ts:714-731 (the whole loser-share validation block) and §10 still passes 4/4, because it never posts either slice. Delete MAX_LOSER_SHARE_RATE and the clamp at payout.ts:476 and §7 still passes, because RATES has no feeModel. Meanwhile the two suites that DO touch high loser-share rates treat them as legitimate operating points and say so in their own comments: fee-model-caption.test.mts:123-124 says "An operator typing 60% + 60% is charged 100% of the losing side, and must be told 100%", and :290 asserts the caption "still fits at the maximum rate an operator can configure" — the repo's own guard naming 100% as the operator's maximum. thin-market-alert.test.mts:239 builds an 80% loser-share profile as a routine scenario with the note "the rate is an operator lever".
findings.rulesReference: RULES.md §2.1 ("Guarded by: npm run test:fee-model … npm run test:loser-share-fee") — the guards RULES names for the 13% rule cannot see the live model's rate at all
findings.concreteScenario: An engineer changing the fee validation runs `npm run predeploy`, which includes test:fee-model and test:loser-share-fee (package.json:218). Setting platformFeeRate to 0.5 and operatorFeeRate to 0.5 in the live config, or removing the sum check entirely, leaves every one of those assertions green — there is no assertion anywhere in scripts/ that a loser-share rate above 13% is refused, warned about, or even noticed. §10's two ceiling assertions and §7's "never more than a third of the prize" assertion are the only two that read as a house-share ceiling, and both read feeCeilingRate / DEFAULT_FEE_CEILING_RATE.
findings.moneyImpact: No direct shillings; this is why LEAD-D.a and LEAD-D.b survived a green predeploy. §7's comment — "The promise we print in the Terms: never more than a third of what you win" — is also stale against RULES §7, which records that /legal/terms §4 was rewritten in all three languages to "13% of the losing side" and the retired-ceiling copy deleted, so the guard is pinning a promise the contract no longer makes.

findings.title: At a configured 100% loser-share rate the pre-bet "possible winnings" headline is arithmetically impossible in every book — nothing ties estimatedWinningsRate to the fee rate
findings.functionName: BetConfirmModal payout disclosure / poolFee loser-share arm
findings.whatTheCodeDoes: The loser-share pre-bet figure is `stake × (1 + estimatedWinningsRate)`, a display-only number read from config and completely decoupled from platformFeeRate/operatorFeeRate. validate() bounds it only by MAX_ESTIMATED_WINNINGS_RATE = 5 and never cross-checks it against the fee. At loserRate = 1.0, settledPayoutFor pays every winner `round((stake/winningPool) × winningPool)` = exactly stake, in every possible book, because netPool == winningPool identically.
findings.whyItIsWrong: RULES §2.1 and COMPLIANCE-DECISIONS accept the estimate as a marketing figure carrying a mandatory disclaimer — an uncertain number, not an impossible one. At a 100% configured rate it stops being uncertain: there is no split of any poll at which any winner receives more than 1.000× stake, so the headline is unachievable rather than optimistic. The disclaimer says the figure is an estimate; it does not say the figure can never occur.
findings.rulesReference: RULES.md §2.1 (the estimate is a display rate, not the pari-mutuel payout) · §2.8 (a player is charged the pool fee and the withdrawal fee and nothing else) — at a 100% take the "pool fee" is the player's entire prize

She reads "TZS 150,000" under the estimated-winnings label. She stakes 100,000, her side wins, and she is paid exactly TZS 100,000 — as is every other winner in every other book on the platform, because the payout ratio is pinned at 1.000 by the rate. On Up & Down the same holds at estimatedWinningsRate 0.4 (updown-config.ts:276): the card advertises × 1.4 and the maximum payable is × 1.000.
findings.moneyImpact: Aisha commits TZS 100,000 against a stated TZS 150,000 upside that cannot occur — a TZS 50,000 headline gap on a single confirm, repeated on every bet placed while the config stands, on both products. This is the player-facing consequence of LEAD-D.a and is entirely conditional on it: at the rule's 13% the estimate is merely optimistic, which RULES accepts.
