findings.title: The idempotency key is looked up globally and unscoped, and a TERMINAL FAILED withdrawal replays as `ok: true` — a genuine retry silently does nothing and is reported as success
findings.whatTheCodeDoes: Lines 1438-1443 look the key up with `db.txn.findByIdempotencyKey`, which is `pc().transaction.findUnique({ where: { idempotencyKey: key } })` (prisma-dal.ts:1510-1512) — no `userId` filter, no `type` filter, no status filter. Any hit at all returns `{ ok: true, data: { txnId, status, fee, net } }` for that row and returns before the schema parse, the provider-pause check, the destination check, the KYC gate, and the debit. The key itself is a plain hidden form field (`idempotency-key-field.tsx:18`, `withdraw/actions.ts:107`) generated once per component MOUNT and deliberately preserved across server re-renders by a `useRef`.
findings.whyItIsWrong: A FAILED withdrawal is not a completed one. `settleWithdrawalFailed` returns the full gross to spendable balance and marks the row FAILED (wallet-service.ts:806-807) — the obligation is live again and the player's next tap is a NEW intent, not a duplicate. Replaying it as `ok: true` means the platform reports success for a payout it never attempted, on the money-out screen. Separately, the lookup is not scoped: nothing ties the key to the caller, so a key belonging to another user's row, or to the same user's DEPOSIT row, resolves and is returned as a withdrawal result.
findings.rulesReference: RULES.md §2.9 (every player-facing refusal states the reason and the next step at a matching severity) — here there is no refusal at all, only a false success
findings.concreteScenario: Player holds TZS 120,000 and requests TZS 50,000. `dispatchWithdrawal` returns PROVIDER_DOWN, `settleWithdrawalFailed` puts the 50,000 back (balance 120,000, hold 0) and marks txn K FAILED. `withdrawAction` redirects to `/wallet/withdraw?error=…` — the SAME route, so the client tree is reconciled rather than remounted and the `useRef` key K survives, which is the exact behaviour the component's own comment relies on. The rail comes back up ten minutes later; the player taps Send funds again. Line 1439 finds row K, line 1442 returns `{ok:true, status:"FAILED", fee:750, net:49250}`. No hold is placed, no dispatch is made, the wallet does not move, and the action redirects to `/wallet?withdrawal=<old id>&status=FAILED`. Every further tap from that page state does the same. The TZS 50,000 is never sent until the player thinks to hard-reload the tab.
findings.moneyImpact: A legitimate TZS 50,000 payout is silently not executed while the service layer returns success. No shillings are destroyed, but the player cannot get their money out and the platform's own return value says the request was handled. On the unscoped half, a crafted POST reusing the player's own DEPOSIT key returns that deposit's id/fee/net as a withdrawal result, and a key belonging to another account leaks that account's transaction id into the redirect URL.

findings.title: The advertised withdrawal minimum (TZS 1,000) is one the platform refuses — the real floor at the live 1.5% rate is TZS 1,015, and 1,000 is stated on three surfaces in three languages
findings.whatTheCodeDoes: `WITHDRAW_MIN_TZS = 1_000` is the schema floor and is also handed to the wallet Limits tab (`wallet/page.tsx:328` → `wallet-client.tsx:658`, rendered as "TZS 1,000 – 5,000,000 per withdrawal") and restated in the withdraw hint copy (`i18n-dict.ts:1104` EN, `:3369` SW, `:5423` ZH). The server then applies a SECOND, higher floor: `if (net < PROVIDER_MIN_PAYOUT_TZS)` at wallet-service.ts:1580, where net = amount − round(amount × 0.015).
findings.whyItIsWrong: At the live rate a TZS 1,000 request nets 985 and is refused. The stated minimum is therefore a number the platform will not honour, and it ships in all three dictionaries and on the Limits tab. The form's own `min` attribute is correct (`Math.max(WITHDRAW_MIN_TZS, minWithdrawalForRate(rate))` = 1,016 at page.tsx:209), so one screen contradicts itself: the input says 1,016 and the hint underneath it says 1,000. This is the same class RULES.md §2.9 records as having shipped in three languages once already.
findings.rulesReference: RULES.md §2.9 (state the reason and the next step; the figure must be the one enforced) and the §7 doctrine that a number written twice will disagree with itself
findings.concreteScenario: Player's balance is TZS 1,200. They read "Min TZS 1,000" on the withdraw hint and on the wallet Limits tab, and request TZS 1,000. fee = Math.round(1000 × 0.015) = 15; net = 985; 985 < PROVIDER_MIN_PAYOUT_TZS (1,000) → refused with "The smallest amount we can send is TZS 1,000 after the fee. Withdraw at least TZS 1,016." They cannot reach 1,016 with a 1,200 balance either — 1,016 is affordable, so they can in fact proceed, but any player holding between TZS 1,000 and TZS 1,014 is permanently unable to withdraw anything while every limits surface tells them 1,000 is enough.
findings.moneyImpact: Balances of TZS 1,000–1,014 are unwithdrawable for the life of the account while the platform advertises otherwise. The loss per player is small; the misstatement is systematic, appears on the wallet Limits tab as a hard cap pair, and is duplicated across EN/SW/ZH.

findings.title: The withdrawal fee has no rule anchor — an officer can save 5% and the platform charges it, with every surface agreeing with itself
findings.whatTheCodeDoes: `withdraw` reads the rate purely from config: `computeWithdrawalFee(amount, wcfg.withdrawalFeeRate)` (wallet-service.ts:1572). The admin door accepts any value in 0–0.05 and compares it to nothing but the gateway share. There is no equivalent of §2.3's `PLATFORM_MIN_STAKE`/`PLATFORM_MAX_STAKE` anchor for this rate.
findings.whyItIsWrong: RULES.md §1 and §2.7 state the withdrawal fee as a RULE — "1.5% of the amount withdrawn" — in the same table as the stake bounds, and §2.3 says of those bounds that "the admin doors validate against these, so the platform cannot be configured out of its own rule: an operator may NARROW the window inside 1,000…1,000,000, never widen it". No such protection exists for the withdrawal fee. `scripts/withdrawal-fee.test.mts:111-115` actively asserts that an officer CAN set 2% and that the player is then charged it, so the one guard that touches this pins the tunability rather than the rule. I flag honestly that §2.7 itself says the rate is "configured in market.config, editable at /admin/config" — so either the law means 1.5% is a default (in which case §1's rule table is the thing that is wrong and should say so), or it means 1.5% is binding (in which case the door is the defect). It cannot be both, and today nothing in code prefers either reading.
findings.rulesReference: RULES.md §1 + §2.7 (withdrawal fee 1.5%), measured against §2.3's own statement that a rule-bearing knob must be anchored so the platform cannot be configured out of its own rule
findings.concreteScenario: A payments officer at /admin/config types 5.00 into the withdrawal-fee field. `setGlobalConfig` accepts it (0.05 is the inclusive ceiling), `persist()` writes the whole snapshot, and every process re-hydrates it via `{ ...DEFAULT_GLOBAL_CONFIG, ...stored.global }`. The next player to withdraw TZS 1,000,000 is charged fee = round(1,000,000 × 0.05) = TZS 50,000 and receives TZS 950,000 instead of the TZS 985,000 the law entitles them to. The confirm modal, the withdraw hint, the txn row, the audit payload and the ledger all agree with each other, because all six read the same config — so the overcharge is invisible to every consistency check in the repo.
findings.moneyImpact: Up to TZS 35,000 taken from a single player on a single 1,000,000 withdrawal beyond what §2.7 permits, repeatable on every withdrawal, platform-wide, from one admin save with no code change and no alarm.

findings.title: The operator retry paths call `withdraw()` with no idempotency key and no lock, so a double-click issues a second real payout and charges the player a second withdrawal fee
findings.whatTheCodeDoes: Both operator paths pass `undefined` as the third argument (the idempotencyKey) and take no lock over the FAILED row. `retryWithdrawalAction` checks `t.status !== "FAILED"` and only marks the row CANCELLED AFTER `withdraw()` has returned; `bulkRetryAction` loops over up to 50 rows read from `db.txn.listByStatus("FAILED")` with the same shape.
findings.whyItIsWrong: The FAILED row is the only interlock and it is not claimed until the payout has already been dispatched. Two concurrent invocations — one operator double-clicking the retry button, or two officers on /admin/payments, or a bulk run overlapping a single-row retry — both read the row as FAILED and both call `withdraw()`. Each call takes its own hold, computes its own fee and dispatches its own payout. Nothing dedupes them, because the one mechanism that would (`idempotencyKey`) is explicitly passed as `undefined`, as the comment at line 316 notes without treating it as a gap.
findings.rulesReference: RULES.md §2.8 (a player is charged the pool fee and the withdrawal fee and NOTHING ELSE) — a second withdrawal fee on a payout the player never requested is a third charge
findings.concreteScenario: A player's TZS 500,000 withdrawal failed on a PROVIDER_DOWN and was auto-refunded, so their balance reads TZS 1,200,000. An officer clicks Retry twice in the same second (the form has no in-flight disable). Both calls pass `t.status === "FAILED"`. Call 1: hold 500,000, fee 7,500, dispatch 492,500. Call 2: balance is now 700,000 so `requireBalanceGte` still passes — hold another 500,000, fee another 7,500, dispatch another 492,500. The player receives TZS 985,000 against a single TZS 500,000 obligation, their balance is down TZS 1,000,000, and they have paid TZS 15,000 in withdrawal fees for one withdrawal they asked for once.
findings.moneyImpact: TZS 7,500 taken from the player as a second withdrawal fee on a 500,000 retry they never requested (1.5% of whatever the original was, so up to TZS 15,000 at the 1,000,000 bound), plus a duplicate real payout to the mobile-money rail that has to be reclaimed by hand. Repeats per extra click, up to 50 rows at a time on the bulk path.

findings.title: adminAdjustBalance refuses a non-ACTIVE wallet in BOTH directions, so the clawback shortfall doctrine points at a tool that cannot debit a frozen wallet
findings.whatTheCodeDoes: After taking the wallet lock it refuses outright unless the wallet is ACTIVE: `if (wallet.status !== "ACTIVE") return { ok: false, error: \`Wallet is ${wallet.status}, not ACTIVE.\`, code: "INVALID" }`. The check is direction-blind — it blocks a debit exactly as it blocks a credit.
findings.whyItIsWrong: Its mirror primitive in the same file takes the opposite position deliberately, and says so: debitInternal, wallet-service.ts:1993-1995 — "Recover what is there, never more. A frozen/closed wallet is still debitable — the money is ours to take back, and freezing it against the partner would be perverse." And the clawback doctrine names `adminAdjustBalance` as the recovery route for what debitInternal could not take: affiliate-service.ts:1396-1399 — "a partner who has already withdrawn the money leaves a DEBT: the row is marked REVERSED ... and the shortfall is audited as a COMPLIANCE row for an officer to recover through the ordinary adjustment path." That path refuses precisely the wallets a recovery case is most likely to involve, because freezing is the first thing compliance does to a partner under suspicion.
findings.rulesReference: none - internal consistency (RULES §2.10 Clawback: "a shortfall is audited as a debt, never silently forgiven" — the debt is recorded, but the named instrument for collecting it refuses)
findings.concreteScenario: Agent A accrued TZS 605 of commission on a settled poll and withdrew it. The poll is voided; `clawbackMarketCommission` calls `debitInternal(A, 605, …)`, which recovers 0 (balance is 0) and audits `affiliate.clawback.shortfall` with `shortfall: 605` for an officer to collect. Compliance freezes A's wallet on the same fraud suspicion. A later deposits TZS 200,000 into that frozen wallet. The officer opens /admin/players/A and submits a debit of 605 with a reason; `adminAdjustBalance` returns "Wallet is FROZEN, not ACTIVE." and moves nothing. The only way to collect is to unfreeze the wallet — dropping the fraud control — debit, and re-freeze, with A free to withdraw in the window between.
findings.moneyImpact: The house cannot recover an audited debt (TZS 605 here, unbounded in general — the clawback runs over every accrual a voided market produced) without first removing the control that is holding the funds in place. The recovery window created by unfreeze→debit→re-freeze is exactly when the counterparty is motivated to withdraw.

findings.title: The agent commission notification and email state the pre-withholding GROSS as the amount that is "in your cash balance", while the wallet received the NET
findings.whatTheCodeDoes: The lock callback returns `{ credited, cut, status }` where `cut` is the capped commission BEFORE withholding (set at line 1310/1323, and only then passed through `splitWithholding` at line 1313). The wallet is credited `split.netTzs` (line 1315) and the ReferralReward row records `amountTzs: split.netTzs` (line 1338). But the notification and the email are both handed `paid.cut` — the gross.
findings.whyItIsWrong: `agentCommissionEarnedHtml` renders that figure as money already in the wallet: "your share of the net fee — {amountTzs} — is in your cash balance as withdrawable money", with a detail row "Commission: {amountTzs} · Paid as: Withdrawable cash" (email.ts:1897-1904). `notifyAgentCommission` does the same: "Credited to your cash balance ... Withdrawable now" (notification-service.ts:1824-1829). Neither is true of the gross. The reversal half of the same programme uses the net (`agentCommissionReversedHtml({ amountTzs: current.amountTzs, … })`, affiliate-service.ts:1367), so the two halves quote different bases for the same money. RULES §2.10's Withholding row is explicit that "The wallet receives the net; the row records gross, tax and net", and the binding terms clause added on 2026-09-08 promises "local withholding tax is deducted from your commission and only the balance reaches your wallet".
findings.rulesReference: RULES.md §2.10 (Withholding: "The wallet receives the net") and §2.9 (a money surface must state what actually happened)
findings.concreteScenario: Agent A, live rate 10%, withholding 5%. Recruit P stakes TZS 100,000; the position's attributable operator-net fee is TZS 6,375 (RULES §2.10's own guard fixture). `grossCut = floor(6375 × 0.10) = 637`; `splitWithholding(637, 5)` → tax 32, net 605. A's wallet receives TZS 605 and the reward row says 605. A is bell-notified and emailed "Agent commission · TZS 637", body "your share of the net fee — TZS 637 — is in your cash balance as withdrawable money", detail row "Commission TZS 637 · Paid as Withdrawable cash". A opens the wallet and finds 605.
findings.moneyImpact: Every accrual overstates the credited amount by the withholding — 5% of gross, TZS 32 on TZS 637 here — on the two surfaces the agent reads first, and understates nothing anywhere else, so the discrepancy always runs in the direction of a partner believing they were short-paid. Across a lifetime, uncapped, on every settled position of every recruit, it is a permanent, repeatable disagreement between what the platform tells a partner it paid and what it paid, and it is the kind of discrepancy that becomes a dispute rather than a rounding note.

findings.title: The hold release has no `requireHoldGte` guard and `hold` is allowed to go negative, which is exactly what makes the trial balance blind to MO-3.a/b/c
findings.whatTheCodeDoes: Every hold release in the withdrawal lifecycle calls `db.wallet.adjust` with `opts` omitted or `undefined`: line 617 `db.wallet.adjust(w.id, { hold: -amt }, undefined, tx)`, line 806 `db.wallet.adjust(w.id, { balance: amt, hold: -amt })`, aml/actions.ts:167 the same. Both store implementations expose a `requireHoldGte` guard that maps to a `WHERE hold >= n` predicate — prisma-dal.ts:1286 `if (opts?.requireHoldGte !== undefined) where.hold = { gte: opts.requireHoldGte };` and store.ts:1122 the memory twin. A repo-wide grep for `requireHoldGte` returns only those two definitions and the two type declarations: it has ZERO call sites.
findings.whyItIsWrong: The detector of record is `computeTrialBalance`, and it compares `walletReal = w.balance + w.hold` against `Σ PLAYER:{userId}` (ledger.ts:767). A duplicated hold-release-plus-credit moves balance and hold by equal and opposite amounts, so walletReal is unchanged and realDrift stays 0 — the trial balance reports ok:true over a wallet that is materially wrong. That construction is correct for an in-flight withdrawal (see cleared claim 6), but it means the ONE thing that would surface MO-3.a/b/c is a `hold < 0` check, and there is none in production. `hold < 0` is asserted only in `src/app/api/dev-test/stress-money/route.ts:83` and in `scripts/money-invariants.test.mts:104` — a suite that runs against the in-memory store (no DATABASE_URL), where `withLock` is a Promise-chain mutex and every write self-applies, so the split-commit window it would need to detect cannot exist there. Wiring `requireHoldGte: amt` and checking the return would have made the second refund a no-op instead of a payment; the mechanism was built and never connected.
findings.rulesReference: none - internal consistency (the ledger's own stated invariant set, ledger.ts:700-701, and the "balances to zero is not integrity" trap)
findings.concreteScenario: Take MO-3.a's TZS 200,000 double refund. Wallet ends at balance 700,000, hold -200,000. Had line 806 read `db.wallet.adjust(w.id, { balance: amt, hold: -amt }, { requireHoldGte: amt })`, the second call's `WHERE hold >= 200000` would match zero rows, updateMany would return count 0, adjust would return null, and no shilling would have moved. Instead the write succeeds unconditionally, hold lands at -200,000, and the nightly `trialBalance()` returns driftingWallets 0 / totalAbsDrift 0 / ok true — a wallet holding TZS 200,000 of platform money passes every automated integrity check the platform has.
findings.moneyImpact: No money is lost by this defect alone — it is the reason the TZS 200,000 (MO-3.a), TZS 150,000 (MO-3.b) and TZS 1,000,000 (MO-3.c) losses are silent and open-ended instead of being caught the same night. It also removes the last cheap defence that would have made a duplicate refund a no-op.

findings.title: The 15-second deposit/payout fast poll takes NO leader lease while the 5-minute sweep beside it does — and the multi-container guard cannot see it
findings.whatTheCodeDoes: `runLifecyclePass` acquires the `lifecycle` leader lease before any chore and returns on standby (line 393). `runDepositPoll` — a SECOND `setInterval` at DEPOSIT_POLL_MS = 15,000 (line 485), which calls `creditConfirmedDeposits` and `settleConfirmedWithdrawals` — has only a module-local `depositPolling` boolean and never calls `acquireLeadership`. A grep of the whole repo shows `acquireLeadership` appears in exactly one non-test call site: lifecycle.ts:393. So on N Railway replicas, N containers re-query the same in-flight deposits and payouts against Selcom every 15 seconds while exactly one runs the 5-minute sweep.
findings.whyItIsWrong: leader.ts:5-14 states the reason the lease exists: "two containers re-querying the same in-flight payments and acting on the answers is how a payout gets dispatched twice". The fast lanes are the highest-frequency thing in the process that re-queries in-flight payments and acts on the answers, and they were left outside. The guard that certifies this — scripts/multi-container.test.mts §3 — anchors every assertion on `runLifecyclePass` (`const passAt = lifecycle.indexOf("export async function runLifecyclePass"); const body = lifecycle.slice(passAt, passAt + 8000);`) and never looks at `runDepositPoll` or at `depositTimer` at all. It would report MULTI-CONTAINER: all passed with the fast lanes running unleased on every replica — its population is blind to half the money timers in the file. I must be explicit about the limit of the harm: I traced both fast lanes to `settlePaymentWebhook` → `settleDepositConfirmed` / `settleWithdrawalConfirmed`, both of which re-read the row's status INSIDE `withLock`, and `withLock` on production is `pg_advisory_xact_lock` (locks.ts:99-145), which serialises across containers. So two containers do NOT double-credit or double-release. What they do is double the signed gateway call volume on Selcom's status endpoints and double the audit/needs-review writes, per 15-second tick.
findings.rulesReference: none - internal consistency (leader.ts's own stated contract, and the multi-container guard's own claim)
findings.concreteScenario: Railway is scaled to 2 replicas during a launch-day traffic spike. 40 deposits of TZS 20,000-500,000 are in flight inside the 10-minute fast window. Every 15 seconds each replica issues 40 signed /checkout/order-status calls plus one per in-flight payout — 160 gateway calls a minute instead of 80. Selcom's per-vendor throttle starts returning HTTP 429/5xx; `selcomVerifyOrder` maps every non-ok response to `{ status: null }` → PENDING, so nothing is credited by the fast lane at all, and every one of those 40 deposits falls out of the 10-minute window uncredited and waits for the 30-minute sweep. Meanwhile a real 985,000 payout's re-query is being crowded out by duplicate polling.
findings.moneyImpact: No double-credit and no double-release (the advisory lock holds). The loss is throughput: under gateway throttling caused by the doubled call volume, every in-flight deposit inside the 10-minute window degrades to 30-minute settlement, which is precisely the wait the fast lane was built (2026-07-20) to remove and which makes players pay twice. It also silently voids the platform's own multi-container safety claim, so the next person who scales to 2 will believe the guard covered them.

findings.title: A 20-minute band where NOTHING re-queries a deposit: the fast lane stops at 10 minutes, the sweep starts at 30 — and the comment claims coverage that does not exist
findings.whatTheCodeDoes: `creditConfirmedDeposits(olderThanMs = 8_000, fastWindowMs = 10 * 60 * 1000)` selects only deposits with `at < now-8s && at >= now-10min`. `reconcileStalePayments(olderThanMs = 30 * 60 * 1000)` selects only `createdAt < now-30min`. Both are called from lifecycle.ts with no arguments (lines 204 and 230), so those defaults are the live values. A deposit aged between 10 and 30 minutes is selected by neither: nothing asks Selcom about it.
findings.whyItIsWrong: The payout lane immediately below states the design rule this violates, in its own header: `settleConfirmedWithdrawals(olderThanMs = 8_000, fastWindowMs = 30 * 60 * 1000)` with the comment "The window is [olderThanMs, fastWindowMs] = [8s, 30min], which meets the stale sweep exactly at its 30-minute cutoff — no gap where nobody is asking, and no overlap where both are." The deposit lane's own comment asserts coverage that does not exist — "A deposit older than that is no longer someone staring at a spinner, and the 5-minute sweep plus the 30-minute reconcile already own it" — but there is no 5-minute-cutoff sweep: the FIVE MINUTES is the CADENCE of `maybePaymentSweeps`, and the only function it runs against deposits carries a THIRTY-minute cutoff. The comment names a control that is not there, which is the class of defect this repo has documented repeatedly.
findings.rulesReference: none - internal consistency (the fast-payout lane's stated 'no gap where nobody is asking' rule, applied to the sibling it was modelled on)
findings.concreteScenario: A player deposits TZS 50,000 by M-Pesa at 10:00:00. The USSD push arrives; they hunt for their PIN and approve at 10:12. Selcom debits them. The callback is lost (the exact 2026-07-20 incident this lane was built for). At 10:12 the row is 12 minutes old, so `creditConfirmedDeposits` has already excluded it (`at >= now - 10min` is false) and `reconcileStalePayments` will not select it until 10:30. Nothing queries Selcom for 18 minutes. The player, watching a spinner with 50,000 gone from their M-Pesa, deposits 50,000 again at 10:20. At ~10:30-10:35 the sweep confirms both and credits 100,000. To return the unwanted 50,000 the player must withdraw it and pay the §2.7 fee: 1.5% × 50,000 = 750 TZS.
findings.moneyImpact: 750 TZS charged to the player per duplicated deposit for a delay the platform caused — a deduction §2.8 does not sanction. Multiplied across every deposit whose provider approval lands 10-30 minutes after initiation, plus the support and chargeback cost of a player who believes their money vanished. The structural cost is that the fast lane silently stops covering the band where the pay-twice behaviour actually happens.

findings.title: leftPending drops a handled:false on the floor in the WITHDRAWAL confirm arm — the exact defect that was fixed eleven lines above it in the deposit arm
findings.whatTheCodeDoes: The deposit CONFIRMED arm was repaired to count a refusal: `if (r.handled) { depositsConfirmed++; clearNeedsReview(t.id); } … else leftPending++;` with a comment explaining exactly why ("⛔ A REFUSAL IS NOT A NO-OP… this counts it so the sweep's own return value stops reporting the money as absent"). The withdrawal CONFIRMED arm, eleven lines below, has the identical shape with NO else: `if (r.handled) { withdrawalsConfirmed++; clearNeedsReview(t.id); }`. When `settlePaymentWebhook` returns `handled:false` here, nothing is counted at all — not `withdrawalsConfirmed`, not `leftPending`.
findings.whyItIsWrong: `handled:false` on this call is not benign. Passing no `amount` makes amount-mismatch unreachable, so the reachable refusal is `contradicted-<status>-now-confirmed` (settlePaymentWebhook lines 946-967): the provider says the payout COMPLETED for a transaction we have already recorded as FAILED or REVERSED — i.e. we have already refunded the player AND the money left the float. That is the single most expensive event this sweep can observe, and the sweep's own per-cycle summary (`payments.reconcile_sweep`, line 1324) reports it as nothing happening. The same silence is what the deposit arm's comment says produced a transaction "counted in no total, in front of nobody".
findings.rulesReference: none - internal consistency (the fix applied to the deposit arm at lines 1260-1268 was not applied to its twin)
findings.concreteScenario: A 300,000 TZS payout has been stuck PROCESSING for two hours. At 14:05 an officer clicks "Return to player" (`reverseStuckPayoutAction`); its own re-query returns PENDING so it proceeds, and `settleWithdrawalFailed` refunds 300,000 and marks the row FAILED. At 14:05:02 the sweep, which had already listed the row as PROCESSING, calls `verifyWithdrawalStatus` and this time Selcom answers 000/SUCCESS. `settlePaymentWebhook({providerRef, status:"CONFIRMED"})` finds the row FAILED, classifies it as contradicted, and returns `{ handled:false, reason:"contradicted-failed-now-confirmed" }`. The sweep counts nothing. The `payments.reconcile_sweep` audit row for that cycle reads depositsFailed 0, withdrawalsReversed 0, depositsConfirmed 0, withdrawalsConfirmed 0, leftPending 0 — while a 300,000 TZS double payment has just been confirmed.
findings.moneyImpact: The money loss itself belongs to the reversal, but the sweep's own return value and its per-cycle audit row actively deny that anything happened — the counters an operator reads every five minutes report zero on the cycle that observed a completed double payment. `settlePaymentWebhook` does write a separate SECURITY row, so the event is not wholly invisible; the defect is that the sweep's summary, the thing built to be the per-cycle truth, says the opposite.

findings.title: settleDepositFailed is the only settle function with no lock and no status-conditional write — it can clobber a credited deposit to FAILED
findings.whatTheCodeDoes: It reads the transaction, checks `t.status !== "PROCESSING"`, then writes `status: "FAILED"` unconditionally — with no `withLock`, no re-read, and no WHERE guard on the update. Every other settle function on this path (`settleDepositConfirmed` line 407, `settleWithdrawalConfirmed` line 598, `settleWithdrawalFailed` line 801) does the read-then-write inside `withLock(`wallet:${userId}`)` and re-reads the status inside it. This is the read-modify-write the whole file is built to avoid.
findings.whyItIsWrong: The function's own doc-comment claims the property it does not have: "Idempotent: only acts while the txn is PROCESSING — which is also what makes the player-facing notification + email below fire EXACTLY ONCE." Between the read at line 572-573 and the write at line 574 there is no serialisation of any kind, so a concurrent `settleDepositConfirmed` (which takes the wallet lock and credits) can commit in that window and then be overwritten to FAILED by this unguarded write. The credit and the ledger DEPOSIT group survive; the transaction row does not.
findings.concreteScenario: A card deposit of TZS 120,000 has been PROCESSING for 40 minutes. At 10:40:00.000 the player finally returns to the return page; `settleDepositFromReturn` re-queries Selcom, gets COMPLETED, and `settleDepositConfirmed` takes the wallet lock and credits 120,000 with a ledger DEPOSIT group, committing at 10:40:00.180. At 10:40:00.050 the leader's sweep had already read the row as PROCESSING; its own re-query (racing a provider that is mid-state-change, or with credentials that just went stale → UNSUPPORTED in TEST money-mode) resolves to a failure and at 10:40:00.220 it writes `status: "FAILED"` unconditionally. The wallet now holds 120,000 with a ledger entry, and the transaction row says FAILED. The player is emailed "Deposit failed · TZS 120,000 — no money was taken" for money that was taken and credited, and the row lands in the /admin/payments FAILED retry queue where `bulkRetryAction` will re-run `deposit()` and push a SECOND 120,000 collection at the player's handset.
findings.moneyImpact: A second 120,000 TZS collection can be initiated against the player through the operator retry queue for a deposit that was already credited; and the wallet/transaction tables contradict each other on a money row (the ledger says credited, the transaction says failed), which is what the reconciliation an auditor reads is built from. No loss on its own, but it is the only unserialised money-state write in the file and it manufactures a false FAILED row that other tools act on.
findings.rulesReference: none - internal consistency (the exactly-once contract this function's own header claims and its three siblings implement)

findings.title: An RG-held deposit reaches the AML queue with no officer alert — notifyAdminsAmlReview accepts "DEPOSIT" but is never called with it
findings.whatTheCodeDoes: `notifyAdminsAmlReview(opts: { txnKind: "WITHDRAWAL" | "DEPOSIT"; … })` is declared with a DEPOSIT variant (notification-service.ts:1446), and `withdraw()` calls it for every ≥1M hold. The RG-suspense arm of `settleDepositConfirmed` writes only an `audit()` row; a repo-wide grep finds exactly one call site and it is hard-coded to `txnKind: "WITHDRAWAL"`.
findings.whyItIsWrong: The only money in the system that the platform holds and does not own arrives in the compliance queue silently. The officer's bell and email — the channel built for exactly this queue — never fire, so the debt's discovery depends on somebody happening to open /admin/aml. Combined with MO-5.a (which then deletes the row) and MO-5.b (which has already told the player it was refunded), there is no moment at which a human is prompted that a player is owed money.
findings.rulesReference: none - internal consistency (the DEPOSIT branch of the platform's own officer-alert API is declared and never used, while the WITHDRAWAL branch beside it fires on every hold)
findings.concreteScenario: Player P's TZS 400,000 self-exclusion deposit is booked to HOUSE:RG_SUSPENSE at 14:05 on a Saturday. No bell, no officer email. The /admin/aml "Pending review" KPI moves 0 → 1, which nobody is watching over a weekend. By contrast a TZS 1,000,000 withdrawal held the same minute pages the compliance team through notifyAdminsAmlReview.
findings.moneyImpact: Delays or prevents the return of 100% of the held deposit (TZS 400,000 in the worked case). It does not itself lose the money, but it removes the only push signal that the money is owed, so it converts MO-5.b's latent debt into one that is likely never noticed.

findings.title: A deposit that can never be terminalised in LIVE money mode consumes the player's RG deposit cap and SOF rolling-30d sum for 30 days, and no operator control can clear it
findings.whatTheCodeDoes: `checkDepositLimit` and the SOF gate both call `sumDepositsSince(userId, cutoff, true)`, which aggregates `status: { in: ["CONFIRMED", "PROCESSING"] }`. In LIVE money mode `reconcileStalePayments` deliberately refuses to terminalise a PROCESSING deposit that has no providerRef (line 1247-1249) or whose provider status is UNSUPPORTED (line ~1272-1278): it only increments `leftPending` and writes one needs-review audit row. Nothing else in the repo can move such a row: `retryDepositAction` and `cancelRefundTxnAction` both require `status === "FAILED"`, and `reverseStuckPayoutAction` refuses anything that is not a WITHDRAWAL.
findings.whyItIsWrong: Counting in-flight deposits against the cap is correct and deliberate (audit C4 — it stops N concurrent deposits each reading a pre-deposit total). The defect is that a row which is structurally unable to leave PROCESSING keeps consuming the cap and the SOF sum for the whole 24h/7d/30d window, and the platform has removed every route to clear it. The refusal the player then reads names a limit they did not actually consume, and the same phantom can push a player over the TZS 5,000,000 rolling SOF gate and block deposits outright until an SOF declaration is accepted.
findings.rulesReference: RULES.md §2.9 (a refusal must state the reason and the next step, at a matching severity — "Daily deposit limit of TZS 100,000 would be exceeded" is not the reason, and "wait 24 hours" is not a next step that works)
findings.concreteScenario: Player P sets a daily deposit limit of TZS 100,000. P deposits TZS 100,000 by M-Pesa. The container is redeployed in the window between `dispatchDeposit` returning and `db.txn.update(txnId, { providerRef })` at wallet-service.ts:360, so the row is PROCESSING with providerRef null. On production `isLiveMoneyMode()` is true, so every 30-minute sweep hits line 1247, increments leftPending and leaves the row PROCESSING for ever. P's next deposit — even the minimum TZS 1,000 — is refused with "Daily deposit limit of TZS 100,000 would be exceeded." for the next 24 hours, and the same row inflates the 30-day SOF sum for a month. No admin screen can fail, cancel or retry it.
findings.moneyImpact: No money is taken by this defect on its own, but the player is refused every further deposit for 24h (daily), 7d or 30d depending on which limit they set, on the strength of TZS 100,000 they may never have been charged; and for a heavy depositor a phantom row pushes the 30-day sum over TZS 5,000,000 and blocks deposits entirely until compliance accepts an SOF declaration. Reachable once per redeploy-during-dispatch or per credential outage.

findings.title: "Cancel & refund" writes an audit note asserting "failed deposit never moved money" onto an RG-held deposit whose money demonstrably moved
findings.whatTheCodeDoes: `cancelRefundTxnAction` accepts any transaction whose status is FAILED, flips it to CANCELLED, and writes a COMPLIANCE-grade audit payload whose `note` is chosen purely on `t.type`: for a DEPOSIT it always records "failed deposit never moved money; record closed". The function's own file header repeats the same assumption: "a failed deposit never moved money, so nothing is minted here."
findings.whyItIsWrong: After MO-5.a an RG-held deposit is FAILED, and it is the one class of FAILED deposit for which money DID move: the ledger holds EXTERNAL:<provider> −amount / HOUSE:RG_SUSPENSE +amount, and the player was really debited by their MNO. The action therefore writes a positive, false statement of fact into the audit stream a regulator reads, on the row that records an unpaid debt to a player, and closes it. Nothing in the action inspects `amlReason` (which still starts with `rg_refund_due_`) or the ledger.
findings.rulesReference: none - internal consistency (the audit record asserts the opposite of what the ledger for that same txnId says)
findings.concreteScenario: Player P's TZS 400,000 RG-held deposit has been rejected in /admin/aml (MO-5.a) and is FAILED. It appears in the failed-payments list on /admin/payments; an officer tidying the queue clicks "Cancel & refund". The row becomes CANCELLED and `payments.cancel_refund` is written with `payload.note = "failed deposit never moved money; record closed"` and `payload.amount = 400000`. The ledger simultaneously carries HOUSE:RG_SUSPENSE +400,000 against that same txnId. The last artefact anyone will find describing this money now says no money existed.
findings.moneyImpact: Does not itself move TZS, but it destroys the evidence trail for the TZS 400,000 the platform is holding and states, in the compliance log, that there is nothing to return. It converts a recoverable debt into an unrecoverable one.

findings.title: The payout callback re-queries the disbursement rail using COLLECTION credentials
findings.whatTheCodeDoes: The handler builds its Selcom environment once, with `const env = selcomEnv();`, and passes that same `env` to BOTH `selcomVerifyOrder` (deposit, correct) and `selcomVerifyPayout` (payout, line 265). Every other payout-status path in the repo uses the disbursement environment instead: `payments.ts:539 verifyWithdrawalStatus` does `const env = selcomDisburseEnv();`, and `selcomAdapter.withdraw` (payments.ts:369) dispatches with `selcomDisburseEnv()`. `selcomDisburseEnv()` resolves `PAYMENT_DISBURSE_URL / _API_KEY / _API_SECRET / _VENDOR_ID / _PIN` with fall-back to the collection values.
findings.whyItIsWrong: The payout was DISPATCHED with the disburse credentials and, if the operator ever splits the float account, is only visible to that account. Asking about it with collection credentials asks the wrong party. If the divergence is in the key/secret the call 401s, `!res.ok` returns null and the payout is simply never confirmed by callback (a silent regression to 30-minute settlement). If the divergence is only `PAYMENT_DISBURSE_URL`, the query goes to the collection host, which can answer 200 with an envelope about a transaction it has never heard of — and per MO-6.b that becomes FAILED and refunds a payout that already left. The file `selcom.ts:63-73` documents that these overrides exist precisely so payouts can move to a separate float account; the webhook is the one caller that was not updated for that day.
findings.rulesReference: none - internal consistency: contradicts the disburse/collection separation documented at src/lib/server/selcom.ts:63-73 and the pattern used by verifyWithdrawalStatus.
findings.concreteScenario: The operator moves payouts to a separate Selcom float account and sets `PAYMENT_DISBURSE_URL` + `PAYMENT_DISBURSE_API_KEY/_SECRET`. A player's TZS 500,000 withdrawal (net 492,500) goes out on the disburse account. Selcom's cashin callback arrives; the handler asks the COLLECTION host about that transid. Best case the collection host 401s and the callback is a no-op, so the payout is confirmed 30 minutes later by the sweep instead of instantly. Worst case the collection host answers 200 with a not-found envelope, `envelopeSettlementVerdict` returns FAILED, and the player gets TZS 500,000 back on top of the 492,500 already on their handset.
findings.moneyImpact: Zero today if no PAYMENT_DISBURSE_* override is set (the two envs are then value-identical); TZS 492,500 double-paid per affected withdrawal on the day the float accounts are split, which is a config change nobody would associate with the webhook.

findings.title: Nothing on the payout side compares the amount Selcom reports against the amount we asked it to send — the M4 tamper check is structurally dead for withdrawals
findings.whatTheCodeDoes: `selcomVerifyPayout` returns only `{ status, detail }`; it never reads an amount out of the envelope, unlike its deposit twin `selcomVerifyOrder` which extracts `const rawAmt = row.amount` and returns `{ status, amount }` (selcom.ts:838-841). Consequently every payout settlement path passes no amount: the webhook's withdrawal branch leaves `amount` undefined (route.ts:247, 273), `settleConfirmedWithdrawals` calls `settlePaymentWebhook({ providerRef: t.providerRef!, status: "CONFIRMED" })` (wallet-service.ts:1158), and the reconcile sweep does the same (wallet-service.ts:1301). `settlePaymentWebhook`'s M4 guard is `if (input.amount != null && Math.abs(input.amount) !== Math.abs(txn.amount))`, so with `amount` always null it can never fire on a withdrawal.
findings.whyItIsWrong: The route's own header advertises "Settlement itself (settlePaymentWebhook) is exactly-once + amount-tamper-defended", and that claim is true only for deposits. Money going OUT is the direction where a disagreement between what we asked and what the gateway did is unrecoverable: we finalise the player's debit at the GROSS amount on the strength of a `000 SUCCESS` that we never check is about the right sum. This is the 'would this still pass if the feature were absent?' shape — the M4 comment and the guard both exist, and for half the money they do nothing.
findings.rulesReference: docs/RULES.md §2.7 / §2.8 — the player is charged the withdrawal fee and nothing else; a payout that delivers less than net while we debit the full gross charges them the difference.
findings.concreteScenario: A player withdraws TZS 1,000,000. Fee 15,000, net 985,000 dispatched with `amount: 985000`. Selcom (a decimal/units slip, a partial delivery, or a manual re-keying by their support during an incident) actually disburses 98,500 and its `/walletcashin/query` envelope reports `resultcode 000` with `amount: 98500`. We read only the result code, mark CONFIRMED, and `settleWithdrawalConfirmed` finalises the debit: the hold of 1,000,000 is released as spent. The player received 98,500 and was charged 1,000,000 — an 886,500 shortfall — and the ledger, the receipt and the Selcom statement page all read as a clean, fully-paid withdrawal.
findings.moneyImpact: The player loses the difference between requested net and delivered amount, silently and with no queue entry — TZS 886,500 in the scenario above. It also removes the only automatic detector we would have of a gateway-side amount error, so the loss is invisible until the player complains.

findings.title: reconcileMatchAction ignores the update result identically — a providerRef an officer types that already exists on the same rail silently no-ops while the action reports success and audits "matched"
findings.whatTheCodeDoes: The officer types a free-text `providerRef` (validated only as `.trim().slice(0, 120)` with `length >= 3`). Nothing checks whether that ref is already carried by another transaction. The write is `await db.txn.update(txnId, { providerRef })` with the return value discarded, followed unconditionally by the COMPLIANCE audit `payments.reconcile.matched` carrying `{ providerRef, reason, type, amount }` and `return { ok: true }`. As in MO-7.b, `@@unique([provider, providerRef])` makes a same-rail duplicate throw P2002, which `db.txn.update` swallows into `null`.
findings.whyItIsWrong: Manually matching a settlement row to a transaction is the control that turns unexplained drift into reconciled money. When it silently does nothing, the officer is told the item is matched, the COMPLIANCE log says it was matched, and the drift figure does not move — so the same item reappears and the officer either re-does it or concludes the reconciliation strip is broken. Separately, because the constraint is `(provider, providerRef)` and not `providerRef` alone, a ref that collides ACROSS rails is accepted, and `db.txn.findByProviderRef` is a `findFirst` with no ordering (prisma-dal.ts:1361-1364) — the webhook at route.ts:243 resolves an incoming Selcom reference through exactly that call, so two rows sharing a ref make the row it settles a coin flip.
findings.rulesReference: none - internal consistency
findings.concreteScenario: An officer reconciling against a Selcom statement types `SLC-2026-09-08-0041` for an unmatched CONFIRMED M-Pesa deposit of TZS 75,000 — the same reference they used ten minutes earlier for an M-Pesa withdrawal of TZS 300,000 (a copy-paste from the wrong statement line). Postgres rejects the duplicate `(MPESA, SLC-2026-09-08-0041)`; `db.txn.update` returns null; the action returns `{ ok: true }`; the modal shows "Matched"; a COMPLIANCE row records `payments.reconcile.matched · providerRef SLC-2026-09-08-0041 · amount 75,000`. The TZS 75,000 deposit remains unmatched and keeps contributing TZS 75,000 to the drift the page insists "must be TZS 0".
findings.moneyImpact: A reconciliation decision recorded against TZS 75,000 that the database never accepted, and TZS 75,000 of unexplained PSP drift left uncleared while the console and the compliance log both say it was cleared. Where the typed ref collides across two different rails instead, the write succeeds and creates a duplicate key that a later Selcom callback resolves non-deterministically through `findByProviderRef`'s `findFirst`.

findings.title: reconcile() counts a write-off as MATCHED and removes its amount from driftTzs, so the console's "Drift must be TZS 0" integrity signal can be zeroed by writing real unmatched money off
findings.whatTheCodeDoes: `reconcile()` partitions confirmed money movements purely on the presence of a `providerRef`: `const matched = money.filter((t) => !!t.providerRef); const unmatched = money.filter((t) => !t.providerRef);` and computes `driftTzs` from the unmatched set only. `reconcileWriteOffAction` writes a synthetic `WRITEOFF-…` string into that same field. There is no third bucket and no filter that excludes the sentinel, so from the reconciliation strip's point of view a write-off and a genuine PSP settlement reference are the same thing. /admin/payments renders `Matched`, `Unmatched`, `Drift`, and the caption "A confirmed movement reconciles when it carries the PSP correlation ref. Drift must be TZS 0." (page.tsx:200).
findings.whyItIsWrong: This is the "ledger sums to zero is not integrity" shape. Drift is the only signal on this console that says our records and the PSP's disagree. Writing an item off does not resolve that disagreement — it declares it unresolvable — yet it moves the money out of `unmatched`, out of `driftTzs`, and INTO `matched`, where it is counted alongside real settlements. The screen an officer consults to answer "do we and Selcom agree?" cannot distinguish "we agree" from "we gave up", and a period with TZS 4,000,000 written off reads identically to a period that reconciled cleanly.
findings.rulesReference: none - internal consistency
findings.concreteScenario: Over a 24h window six confirmed M-Pesa deposits totalling TZS 1,800,000 have no PSP reference (a webhook outage left them credited by the fast-credit poll with the ref write failing). The strip reads `Matched 214 · Unmatched 6 · Drift TZS 1,800,000` in danger red, with an "Investigate" link. An officer writes all six off. The strip now reads `Matched 220 · Unmatched 0 · Drift TZS 0` in the ok tone — the exact reading a genuinely reconciled day produces. Nothing on the page, and nothing in `reconcile()`'s return shape, records that TZS 1,800,000 of the "matched" total is a sentinel.
findings.moneyImpact: TZS 1,800,000 of unexplained difference between our ledger and the PSP is rendered invisible on the one console that exists to surface it, and is reported as reconciled. Any downstream reader of that strip — including the officer deciding whether to escalate to Selcom before the settlement window closes — is given a clean bill for money nobody has accounted for.

findings.title: Neither retry path passes an idempotency key and neither holds a per-row claim, so two concurrent clicks on one FAILED row dispatch two real money movements — the player paths pass a key, the officer paths pass undefined
findings.whatTheCodeDoes: Both single-row retries and the bulk loop read the row with `db.txn.findById`, check `status === "FAILED"`, then call `deposit()` / `withdraw()` with the idempotency argument explicitly `undefined` — the withdrawal path even says so in a comment: "`undefined` is the idempotencyKey this path has never passed." The FAILED row is not claimed, locked or transitioned before dispatch; it is only updated to CANCELLED after the new movement returns. The player-facing paths do the opposite: `deposit/actions.ts:122-123` and `withdraw/actions.ts:107-112` both read `formData.get("idempotencyKey")` and pass it through, and `deposit()`/`withdraw()` each re-check that key inside the wallet lock precisely to make a double-tap exactly-once (wallet-service.ts:71-78, 1437-1445, 1601-1604). So the guard the 2G double-tap gets is the guard the money console does not.
findings.whyItIsWrong: The bulk path does not skip a guard the single path has — both skip the guard the PLAYER path has, and the bulk path additionally races itself against any officer clicking a single-row Retry at the same time. `bulkRetryAction` takes no lease of any kind, so two officers (or one officer in two tabs, or a Retry-all overlapping a per-row Retry) both read the same FAILED snapshot and both dispatch. Nothing in `retryDepositAction`/`retryWithdrawalAction`/`bulkRetryAction` re-reads the row's status inside a transaction before dispatching.
findings.concreteScenario: A FAILED M-Pesa deposit of TZS 200,000 for player P sits in the queue. Officer A clicks the row's "Retry"; three seconds later, while A's gateway call is still in flight, Officer B clicks "Retry all". Both read `t.status === "FAILED"`. Both call `deposit(P, { provider: "MPESA", amount: 200_000, msisdn })` with no idempotency key. Two PROCESSING rows are created and Selcom pushes TWO USSD collection prompts to P's handset for TZS 200,000 each. P approves both — the prompts are identical and look like a retry of the one they were expecting. TZS 400,000 leaves their M-Pesa; TZS 400,000 is credited to a wallet for which they authorised one TZS 200,000 deposit. On the withdrawal side the same race on a FAILED payout of TZS 300,000 for a player holding TZS 900,000 spendable produces two debits of TZS 300,000 and two payouts of TZS 295,500 net to the same handset for one request.
findings.moneyImpact: A player's mobile-money account is debited TZS 400,000 against a single TZS 200,000 authorisation, or receives two payouts of TZS 295,500 against a single TZS 300,000 withdrawal request. The ledger balances in both cases — the harm is an unauthorised second money movement on a player's account, initiated by staff, with two `deposit.initiated` / `withdraw.initiated` records where the player consented to one. On the withdrawal side that is a second payout above the amount the player asked for, which is an AML-reportable event.
findings.rulesReference: none - internal consistency (RULES §2.8 is not breached — no extra FEE is taken; the defect is an unrequested duplicate movement, not a charge)

findings.title: Retrying a FAILED CARD deposit can never succeed — no card context is passed — and every attempt mints a fresh FAILED row, so "Retry all" grows the queue instead of clearing it
findings.whatTheCodeDoes: `DepositProvider` in this file explicitly includes `"CARD"` (line 23) and both retry paths call `deposit(t.userId, { provider: (t.provider ?? "MPESA") as DepositProvider, amount, msisdn })` with only two arguments — the 4th parameter `card?: CardCheckoutContext` is never supplied. `selcomAdapter.deposit` refuses immediately on that: `if (provider === "CARD") { if (!card) return { ok: false, reason: "DECLINED", correlationId }; … }` (payments.ts:333-338). Crucially, by the time dispatch runs, `deposit()` has already created a PROCESSING transaction row inside the wallet lock (wallet-service.ts:279-300); on `!result.ok` it marks that new row FAILED (wallet-service.ts:347). The retry action then leaves the ORIGINAL row FAILED too, appending "· bulk retry refused: …" to its description. `retryQueue()` and `bulkRetryAction` both read `db.txn.listByStatus("FAILED")` with no time window, so both rows are in the queue for the next run.
findings.whyItIsWrong: The single-row comment claims the refused case creates nothing: "Retry refused (kill-switch, KYC, rate limit, bounds) — no replacement txn was created, so the FAILED row must stay in the queue." That is true only for the pre-dispatch refusals it lists. A refusal that reaches the adapter — which is every CARD retry, and every PROVIDER_DOWN/DECLINED on a mobile rail — happens AFTER the row exists, so a replacement txn IS created and IS marked FAILED. The queue therefore doubles on each bulk run for every persistently-refusing row, and CARD rows refuse deterministically and forever. This also means the operator's clean-up tool makes the thing it is cleaning up worse, and each new row is a real gateway call against a rail the code has already decided cannot succeed.
findings.rulesReference: none - internal consistency
findings.concreteScenario: Ten card deposits of TZS 100,000 each failed during a Selcom hosted-checkout outage. The retry queue shows 10 rows. An officer clicks "Retry all". For each row `deposit()` runs every gate, creates a PROCESSING txn, dispatches, gets `DECLINED` (no `card` context), and marks the new txn FAILED. The overlay reports "Bulk retry finished with failures · 0 dispatched · 10 still failed". The queue now shows 20 rows. A second click makes it 40, a third 80 — 10 → 20 → 40 → 80, doubling every run, each doubling costing 50 sequential gateway calls and 50 more Transaction rows on the money table.
findings.moneyImpact: No shillings are lost or paid, but the operator's only bulk remediation tool is guaranteed to fail on card rows and to double the failed-payment queue each time it is used, permanently polluting the Transaction table with synthetic FAILED money rows that every reconciliation, report and retry-queue read afterwards has to walk. Once the queue exceeds 50, bulkRetryAction's `.slice(0, 50)` means genuinely retryable mobile-money rows can be crowded out of every run by self-generated card rows.

findings.title: An officer-initiated deposit retry is audited with actorId = the PLAYER — the exact attribution defect the withdrawal retry passes a 4th argument to prevent
findings.whatTheCodeDoes: `withdraw()` takes a 4th `actorId` parameter and both retry paths pass `g.userId` for it, with a comment stating exactly why: "`withdraw()` records who initiated it; without this argument the compliance record would name the PLAYER for an action an officer took", and in the bulk loop "an unattributed run would put the operator's decision behind 50 player names." `deposit()` has no such parameter — its signature is `deposit(userId, input, idempotencyKey?, card?)` — and it writes `audit({ category: "WALLET", action: "deposit.initiated", actorId: userId, … })` (wallet-service.ts:322) plus `deposit.failed` / `deposit.pending` / `deposit.confirmed` all keyed on the player. So every deposit an officer re-initiates from /admin/payments is recorded in the audit log as the player having initiated it, and the officer's own record is a single `payments.retry.deposit` row (or, for bulk, one `payments.retry.bulk` row with only counts and no txn ids).
findings.whyItIsWrong: The repo has already identified this exact failure mode and fixed it on the withdrawal path in the same function block, twice, in writing — and left the deposit path doing the thing the comments forbid. On a licensed platform the question "who caused this money movement?" must have one answer, and here the answer the ledger gives for an officer-caused collection is the player's own id. For the bulk path the officer's audit row carries `{ attempted, retried, stillFailed }` and `targetType: null, targetId: null`, so there is no join from the officer's decision to the specific deposits it re-initiated at all.
findings.rulesReference: none - internal consistency (RULES §5 step 6; the audit record must be readable off the database as what happened)
findings.concreteScenario: A player's TZS 200,000 M-Pesa deposit failed on 2026-08-02 and has sat in the all-time FAILED queue since. On 2026-09-09 an officer clicks "Retry all" to tidy the queue. `deposit()` re-runs for that row and writes `deposit.initiated · actorId: usr_player…` dated 2026-09-09. A fresh USSD prompt lands on the player's handset for TZS 200,000, five weeks after they last tried. If they approve it, the WALLET audit trail says the player initiated a TZS 200,000 deposit that day; the only trace of the officer is one `payments.retry.bulk` row saying `attempted: 47, retried: 31, stillFailed: 16`, with no transaction ids.
findings.moneyImpact: TZS 200,000 of a player's money is collected on a staff decision that the money record attributes to the player. For a bulk run the misattribution scales to every deposit row in that batch — up to 50 — with no way to reconstruct which movements the officer caused. In a dispute or an AML review the platform cannot show, from the ledger, that it did not initiate the collection.

findings.title: `creditInternal` — the agent-commission payout — is the only house→player money-out path whose ledger group is fire-and-forget outside the money transaction, while its own clawback mirror is atomic
findings.whatTheCodeDoes: Inside `withLock('wallet:'+userId)`, line 1888 calls `db.wallet.adjust(wallet.id, { balance: amount })` with NO tx argument, so (prisma-dal.ts:1281 `const db: Db = tx ?? pc();`) it self-commits on a pooled connection; line 1893 self-commits the Transaction row the same way; then line 1924 fires `postLedgerEntries(...)` with no `tx` and no `await`, swallowing any rejection. Three independent commits, the last of them unawaited. Every other money-out path in the file wraps the same three writes in `withMoneyTx` and passes `tx` into `postLedgerEntries`: `settleDepositConfirmed` (line 472), `settleWithdrawalConfirmed` (line 621), `debitInternal` (line 2017), `adminAdjustBalance` (line 2095).
findings.whyItIsWrong: `withMoneyTx`'s contract (ledger.ts:31-40) is that "any throw inside rolls the WHOLE movement back, so the ledger can never be written without the wallet move (or vice versa)". Agent commission is, by RULES §2.10, "Real, **withdrawable cash**" — a real recurring outflow from the house. It is the one such path left outside that contract. The comment at 1916 still calls it a legacy "Dual-write … (fire-and-forget)" from when this function only paid affiliate/proposal rewards; the 2026-09-07/08 agent programme was bolted onto the same line without moving it inside a money tx. `postLedgerEntries`'s own retry+audit path is not a substitute: it does not run at all if the process is replaced before the unawaited promise resolves.
findings.rulesReference: none - internal consistency (ledger.ts:31-40 `withMoneyTx` atomicity contract, audit C3), against RULES.md §2.10 which makes agent commission real withdrawable cash with its own house account.
findings.concreteScenario: An approved agent's recruit settles a poll: losing side TZS 1,000,000 (ten bets of 100,000), fee 130,000, TRA 13,000, GBT 6,500, operatorNet 110,500, agent gross 11,050, withholding 553, net 10,497. `onRecruitSettlement` → `creditWallet` → `creditInternal(agentId, 10_497, { type: 'AGENT_COMMISSION', taxWithheld: 553 })`. Line 1888 commits +10,497 to the agent's wallet and line 1893 commits the AGENT_COMMISSION Transaction. The container is replaced (every push to main deploys live) before the unawaited insert at 1924 lands, or the three `createMany` attempts all fail. HOUSE:AGENT_COMMISSION is never debited 11,050, PLAYER:{agent} never credited 10,497, HOUSE:TAX never credited 553. If that market is later voided, `clawbackMarketCommission` → `debitInternal` posts the exact mirror INSIDE `withMoneyTx` (line 2017): HOUSE:TAX finishes at −553 and HOUSE:AGENT_COMMISSION at +11,050.
findings.moneyImpact: TZS 10,497 of withdrawable cash sits in an agent's wallet with no ledger evidence — a permanent trial-balance drift on that wallet, and the TZS 553 of withholding tax owed to TRA is never booked, so the statutory pack under-remits by it. After a clawback the house book reports the agent programme as a TZS 11,050 PROFIT and HOUSE:TAX as a negative liability, while `reconcileLedger` reports zero imbalanced groups because each group written did sum to zero.

findings.title: The earnings waterfall subtracts the NET agent commission from a GROSS fee, so `netRetained` overstates the owner's earnings by every shilling of agent withholding tax
findings.whatTheCodeDoes: `readWaterfall` computes `agentCommissionOut` as `SUM(amount) … WHERE entryType = 'AGENT_COMMISSION' AND account LIKE 'PLAYER:%'`, i.e. the NET that reached the partner's wallet. `waterfall()` then computes `netRetained: input.feeEarned - input.leviesOut - input.bonusCost - input.agentCommissionOut` (house-book.ts:340). But `agentCommissionEntries` (ledger.ts:575-578) debits the house side by the GROSS (`amount + tax`) and splits it two ways — net to PLAYER, tax to HOUSE:TAX. The house's cost is the gross; only the net is subtracted.
findings.whyItIsWrong: The comment justifying the PLAYER-side read (house-ledger.ts:246-248) says the two sides are "the same money". That was true before management's 2026-09-08 amendment and is false now: the file's own contract at ledger.ts:565-568 says in capitals "⛔ THE HOUSE SIDE MUST CARRY THE GROSS, NOT THE NET. Debiting `HOUSE:AGENT_COMMISSION` by only the net would understate what the programme costs by the whole tax line in the owner's book" — and that is exactly what the waterfall then does, one file over, by reading the player side. Note this is the OPPOSITE asymmetry from `housePosition`, which reads the account balance (`netRetained: commission + agentCommission`, house-book.ts:162) and therefore does carry the gross correctly. The two surfaces on the same page disagree about the same programme by the withholding tax.
findings.rulesReference: RULES.md §2.10 ("**Withholding** … 5% of the agent's gross commission … deducted at accrual and remitted to `HOUSE:TAX`") and §2.2 (a levy is the state's money, never the owner's).
findings.concreteScenario: In one reporting window one approved agent accrues on ten settled positions. Take the same poll as above repeated ten times: each accrual is gross 11,050, withheld 553, net 10,497. `agentCommissionOut` reads the PLAYER side and returns 104,970. `waterfall()` computes netRetained = feeEarned − leviesOut − bonusCost − 104,970. The programme actually cost the house 110,500 (ten × 11,050): 104,970 to the partner and 5,530 remitted to TRA out of HOUSE:TAX.
findings.moneyImpact: The /admin/house Earnings tab overstates the owner's net retained by TZS 5,530 in that window — 5% of every shilling of agent commission, every window, permanently. The Position tab on the SAME page reports it correctly (gross), so the owner is shown two different answers to "what did the agent programme cost" with nothing flagging the difference.

findings.title: The withdrawal fee is frozen on the transaction but its gateway share is RECOMPUTED from live config at confirmation, two lines under a comment forbidding exactly that
findings.whatTheCodeDoes: At initiation (line 1571-1573) `withdraw()` computes both `fee` and `gatewayShare` from live config, but only `fee` is persisted — the Transaction model has no gatewayShare column (schema.prisma has `taxWithheld` at 573 and no gateway field). At confirmation, `settleWithdrawalConfirmed` reads `const fee = t.fee ?? 0;` back from the row and then recomputes `gatewayShare` from `getEffectiveConfig()` as it stands at confirm time, falling back to 0 if that read rejects. Both numbers are handed to `withdrawalEntries`, which splits the frozen fee into HOUSE:AGGREGATOR (gatewayShare) and HOUSE:COMMISSION (the remainder).
findings.whyItIsWrong: The comment immediately above states the law — "The fee was frozen onto the txn row at initiation — read it back, never recompute (a rate change mid-flight would reprice a withdrawal in flight)" — and the next three lines recompute the other half of the same split from live config. RULES §2.7 defines the gateway share as a fixed component of the fee ("0.5 percentage points of it is the gateway's"), so the split of a frozen fee must be frozen with it. `validateConfig` (market-config.ts:619-622) only enforces `gs <= wf` at the moment of the save; it cannot know about an in-flight withdrawal whose fee was frozen at an older, higher rate.
findings.rulesReference: RULES.md §2.7 — withdrawal fee 1.5% of the amount withdrawn, of which 0.5 percentage points is the gateway's.
findings.concreteScenario: A player withdraws TZS 1,000,000 (the §2.3 upper bound). At initiation the fee is frozen at 15,000 (1.5%) and the gateway's slice is 5,000 (0.5%); only the 15,000 is stored. The payout goes PROCESSING on a real async rail. Before the webhook confirms, an officer saves withdrawalFeeRate 1.5% → 1.0% and withdrawalGatewayShareRate 0.5% → 1.0% — both pass validation (each ≤ 5%, and gs ≤ wf). `settleWithdrawalConfirmed` reads fee = 15,000 from the row but recomputes gatewayShare = round(1,000,000 × 0.01) = 10,000. `withdrawalEntries` books HOUSE:AGGREGATOR +10,000 and HOUSE:COMMISSION +5,000.
findings.moneyImpact: TZS 5,000 of operator revenue on a single withdrawal is booked as a payable to the payment gateway that the gateway never charged. `housePosition` then subtracts it from free cash as `aggregatorPayable` and the earnings waterfall omits it from `feeEarned`, so the owner is understated by 5,000 per affected in-flight withdrawal. The group still sums to zero and no guard notices. The player is unaffected — the fee they paid is the frozen one, per §2.7. Also, the `.catch(() => null)` at line 607 makes gatewayShare 0 on any config-read rejection, booking the WHOLE fee to HOUSE:COMMISSION and nothing to the gateway.

findings.title: HOUSE:RG_SUSPENSE can only ever be credited — there is no ledger path for the return it exists to promise, so a returned deposit stays on the books as both cash held and a debt owed
findings.whatTheCodeDoes: `rgSuspenseEntries` posts EXTERNAL:{provider} −amount / HOUSE:RG_SUSPENSE +amount when a deposit lands after the player self-excluded (called from wallet-service.ts:447-451, atomically, correctly). `acct.rgSuspense` appears nowhere else in the source: a repo-wide grep for `acct.rgSuspense` / `HOUSE:RG_SUSPENSE` returns only this credit, the account constant, the two admin page labels, `readHouseAccounts`, and comments. There is no debit helper and no caller that discharges the balance when the money is actually returned to the player.
findings.whyItIsWrong: The account's own docstring (ledger.ts:181-186) says the money "has not been returned yet (that needs the outbound disbursement rail)" and "a non-zero balance here is money we owe a player". The return itself is performed out of band by an officer. When it happens, nothing debits HOUSE:RG_SUSPENSE and nothing credits EXTERNAL — so the ledger permanently asserts both that the platform still holds the cash (`readCustodialCash` negates Σ EXTERNAL, so the −amount stays in railBacked) and that it still owes it. This is the lane's named failure exactly: an account that only ever receives and never releases. The two errors cancel inside `freeHouseCash`, which is why no arithmetic guard would fire, but each figure is individually wrong and the compliance signal the account was built to be — "we owe a self-excluded player money" — becomes permanently and falsely on.
findings.rulesReference: none - internal consistency (ledger.ts:181-186, which defines the account as a temporary holding for money to be returned).
findings.concreteScenario: A player self-excludes. A TZS 200,000 M-Pesa deposit initiated beforehand lands afterwards. `settleDepositConfirmed` takes the RG branch and posts EXTERNAL:MPESA −200,000 / HOUSE:RG_SUSPENSE +200,000, and the txn goes AML_REVIEW so a human sees it. Weeks later an officer wires the 200,000 back to the player from the bank. No code path records that. Forever after, /admin/house reports railBacked custodial cash TZS 200,000 higher than the platform actually holds, and prints "Held for a self-excluded player  −200,000" on the position-derivation table (page.tsx:488) for a debt that was settled.
findings.moneyImpact: TZS 200,000 of cash the platform no longer holds is reported as held, and TZS 200,000 of debt already discharged is reported as owed. `freeHouseCash` is right only because the two errors are equal and opposite; every other figure on the page — custodial cash by counterparty, the RG suspense line, the standing compliance signal — is wrong by the full amount, per returned deposit, permanently. The same shape applies to HOUSE:TRA_LEVY, HOUSE:GBT_LEVY and HOUSE:AGGREGATOR, which are also credit-only with no remittance leg.
